subsubtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF REPORT OF LAW REFORM COMMISSION-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the latest report of the Law Reform Commission which recommends the abolition from the Criminal Code of such offences as incest, abortion, drug offences, obscenity, pornography and acts of indecency, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander):
That this report on our criminal law be referred immediately for study to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs due to the ramifications of these proposals and the fact that the Minister of Justice has stated that he intends to introduce legislation to implement some of the Law Reform Commission's recommendations.

speechtext:

The evidence of a deterioration in rail freight and express service in the province of Newfoundland prompts the need for an investigation into the terms of union between Canada and that province.
I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath):
That this House order a public inquiry be initiated into the CNR's future objectives to ensure adequate service in that province and to allow for the province's participation in over-all transportation policy for Canada.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED SETTLEMENT OF NEGOTIATIONS WITH AIRCRAFT SAFETY INSPECTORS AND CHECKING OF PILOTS' LICENCES- MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43 I ask for the unanimous consent of the House to move a motion on an important matter of pressing necessity.
In view of the fact that aircraft safety inspectors walked out at major airports in Ontario and Quebec last Friday as a result of a breakdown in wage negotiations and that this is a possible first step toward a nationwide work stoppage which could affect airline service, and furthermore, since the Department of Transport is aware that 11 Air Canada pilots are flying with invalid licences as a result of unauthorized company check flights, which not only contravenes section 400 of the air regulations but also creates a safety hazard, and in light of the fact that commercial airline licences are expiring at the rate of 100 per day, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Hnatyshyn):
That the President of the Treasury Board become personally involved in the negotiations between the aircraft safety inspectors and the Ministry of Transport, that the Minister of Transport take the necessary action to guarantee that no pilots are flying with invalid licences as a result of unauthorized checks and that section 400 of the air regulations is strictly enforced with no extensions.

subtopic: LOCKHEED CONTRACT-POSSIBILITY OF OBTAINING DETAILS FROM UNITED STATES CONCERNING BRIBES
LOCKHEED CONTRACT-POSSIBILITY OF OBTAINING DETAILS FROM UNITED STATES CONCERNING BRIBES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I, too, address my question to the Minister of National Defence. Last Thursday, when I questioned him about pay-offs by Lockheed connected with the purchase of aircraft, he suggested I was inviting him to engage in a kind of witch hunt and that there ought to be no investigation until there is something definite to investigate. I understand that the minister is seeking information in writing from Washington. Can we now assume that there is something definite to investigate?

speakeroldname: Hon. James Richardson (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: LOCKHEED CONTRACT-POSSIBILITY OF OBTAINING DETAILS FROM UNITED STATES CONCERNING BRIBES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, of course, we are holding conversations with senior officials of the United States government. As indicated previously, we want their assurances about the financial stability of the Lockheed company. We are also talking about industrial benefits to Canada and about moving production tooling and equipment to this country. We want assurances on those things. As I said only last week, I wanted written confirmation from the United States government before proceeding with this contract, but I did not say that, in those discussions, we were trying to find out if improper payments had been made. We are dealing with at least three departments of the United States government and if improper payments have been made, or there is something about which they want to tell us, I am sure they will tell us. subtopic: LOCKHEED CONTRACT-POSSIBILITY OF OBTAINING DETAILS FROM UNITED STATES CONCERNING BRIBES
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. speechtext: Might I direct a further question to the Minister of National Defence and ask him whether or not Mr. Crutchlow or any other individual in his department or in the Department of Supply and Services entered into any contract calling for the expenditure of any funds up to this point in time which was not properly authorized and if that is the situation, as has been reported, is this a factor which is holding up the signing of the final contract with Lockheed?

speechtext: My question is directed to the Minister of National Defence. I should like to know what other items are holding up the transaction with Lockheed apart from the question of interim financing.

speakeroldname: Hon. James Richardson (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: LOCKHEED CONTRACT-REASONS FOR DELAY IN SIGNING, OTHER THAN FINANCING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is the interim financing or shortterm financing that is the primary problem. As is widely known, shortly after that problem emerged the Lockheed company got into difficulties as a result of accusations concerning improper payments in other parts of the world. subsubtopic: POSSIBILITY OF REDUCTION OR INCREASE IN CHEESE IMPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, I shall put my question to his parliamentary secretary.
In view of the demonstration held by the producers of industrial milk of Canada at noon today, and bearing in mind the representations they made about their problems with regard to their product, I should like to ask, first, whether the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce works in conjunction with the Department of Agriculture with regard to cheese imports, and second, whether those imports will decrease or increase in the coming dairy year? If so, could the minister tell the House why this should be so?

speakeroldname: Mr. Marcel Roy (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: POSSIBILITY OF REDUCTION OR INCREASE IN CHEESE IMPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this morning I met representatives of the Agricultural Producers' Union and industrial milk producers. We reviewed the whole policy of cheese imports and I assured the producers that there will be no increase in the import of cheeses already produced in Canada, especially cheddar. In addition, we looked into the possibility of meeting at some time to study production techniques of cheeses that could be made here in Canada, so that after having established our manufacturing potential, we can adjust an import program instead of our Canadian production.
I am pleased to tell the hon. member that we are working in close co-operation with the Department of Agriculture for we have announced a cheese quota of 50 million pounds for the current year, as was announced by the Department of Agriculture. Before closing, I wish to assure the producers that the imports of any type of cheese manufactured in Canada will not be increased in the next few years.

speechtext: The House resumed, from Friday, March 26, consideration of the motion of Mr. Macdonald (Rosedale) that Bill C-89, to amend the Anti-Inflation Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO ADD NEW DEFINITIONS
speechtext: When this bill was last before the House, the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) raised a point of order. It was indicated by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) and by the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Blais) that they would like an opportunity to consider the matter. Indeed, the Chair was seeking an opportunity to consider the matter in order, first, that argument on the other side of the question might be presented and, of course, that the Chair would have time to examine the matter to see whether the point of order was in fact valid. It might be appropriate at this time if the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council made a contribution to the argument, or the Minister of Finance, as the case may be. Then we could hear the hon. member for Edmonton West, and then perhaps I would try to make a decision.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO ADD NEW DEFINITIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in due course will I have an opportunity to reply to the reply?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO ADD NEW DEFINITIONS
speechtext: I suppose, in fairness the hon. member for Edmonton West who seeks to clarify something he said on Friday last, he might conclude remarks.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO ADD NEW DEFINITIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think this might help clear up the situation. The question arises concerning the point I raised about the power of the Minister of Finance to enter into an agreement to disperse funds paid into the consolidated revenue fund. This question arises out of this particular bill and has reference to Bill C-73. This matter was not considered by the House, it was not raised and Bill C-73 has been passed by parliament. However, I want to point out that the agreement
March 29, 1976

with the province of Ontario signed by the Minister of Finance was tabled only in mid-January after the bill had been passed. Parliament had no opportunity to determine what kind of model agreement could be entered into by the minister. There is nothing in Bill C-73 which applies to the share of any revenue.
Now I come back. Does parliament at this stage have the opportunity to authorize the minister to enter into such an agreement providing for the payment out? There is no doubt the minister is empowered under the bill to enter into an agreement with a province with regard to the anti-inflation measure, but the minister has no power whatsoever to pay out moneys under any formula, to any province, out of the consolidated revenue fund.
If that power is to exist, it must come by way of a recommendation from His Excellency. That was not provided for in the recommendation to Bill C-73. I do not care whether the minister claims he has power under Bill C-73. There is nothing in the recommendations concerning payment of the funds to a province.
Does this bill relate at all? Yes. First of all, this is a bill to amend the Anti-Inflation Act. Second, Bill C-89 has direct reference to section 4 of the Anti-Inflation Act, Bill C-73. There is, under section 4 of the Anti-Inflation Act, the power to enter into agreements. I refer to page 6 of Bill C-73, particularly to section 4(3). May I say I am not relying upon the first minor amendment that appears in the present bill. However, let us look at clause 6 of this particular bill which amends section 20 of the Anti-Inflation Act. May I say, Mr. Speaker, that there we are right into the heart of the matter. Section 20(4) of Bill C-73, the Anti-Inflation Act, provides:
Where a person has contravened the guidelines by paying or crediting as compensation in the course of a business or as a dividend, an amount that exceeds the amount that he was, under the guidelines authorized to so pay or credit, the administrator may, if he is not satisfied that there are circumstances that, based on the particular facts of the situation, justify the person in so contravening the guidelines, make such order as he deems appropriate to accomplish either or both of the following objectives:
Then paragraph (b) states:
-where no order has been made by him pursuant to subsection (5) arising out of the same circumstances, to require the person to pay to Her Majesty in right of Canada or to withhold out of subsequent payments or credits of a like nature and pay to Her Majesty in right of Canada, an amount stated in the order equal to the whole or any portion of the excess payment or credit as estimated by the administrator.
That is the amount required to be paid to the government of Canada under the order of the administrator. Then there is the model agreement signed by the minister with the province which takes the amount paid under the order of the administrator and divides it with the province on some formula. This formula, this amendment in Bill C-89 is directly connected with that matter. As a matter of fact, section 20(4) (b) is repealed, and in addition sections 20(5) (b), 29(6) and 20(7) are repealed and replaced by sections of clause 6 in Bill C-89. It is precisely under these subparagraphs that the administrator's orders are made.
I ask: How can there be any greater and more direct connection between the two bills? Therefore, it is at this point there should be in the amending bill a provision that any moneys paid to the account of Her Majesty pursuant to
Anti-Inflation Act
such an order may be divided between the government of Canada and a province according to whatever agreements exists. For that there would have to be a recommendation from His Excellency. That is precisely the point I make. There is no recommendation. There is no power to share those moneys with a province under the amendments contained in Bill C-89 which amends Bill C-73. I think I have established the argument to make the connection between Bill C-89 and Bill C-73.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO ADD NEW DEFINITIONS
speechtext: Order, please. It may not be necessary for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) to contribute to the point. As I understand the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), whenever an agreement is made between the federal government and the Minister of Finance with a province, it may be without statutory authorization.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO ADD NEW DEFINITIONS
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO ADD NEW DEFINITIONS
speechtext:
If I understand the point correctly, it might have been authorized in Bill C-73, but in any case it is not dealt with in Bill C-89. The hon. member for Edmonton West, if I understand his point correctly, indicates that the provisions he has just referred to, which I have read very carefully, do not authorize the establishment of any agreement for the sharing of revenue.
It is a matter of fact. Surely, therefore, since they do not propose to do such a thing, no recommendation is required in the statute. The point raised by the hon. member for Edmonton West, that the purported agreement is without statutory foundation, may be valid. The argument that there is no statutory foundation for it in Bill C-73 and, therefore, that there cannot be any foundation for it in the amendments, may be valid; I do not know. Yet the amendments contained in Bill C-89 do not in any way touch on provisions which would relate to any such agreement. I have read these provisions carefully. I would welcome it if the hon. member for Edmonton West could indicate any instance in which such agreements are affected and, if so, in what way they are affected by this particular statute so as to require the royal recommendation.
The hon. member argues that if this statute proposed authorization for the entering into of such agreements, it would require the royal recommendation. In fact, it does not do that and the act does not do that. However, if it were proposed that it should do so, a royal recommendation would have to accompany the act.
I do not have to judge whether the entering into of agreements with provinces is, first, authorized by statutes which in turn must be accompanied by a royal recommendation, but I have to decide, first, if Bill C-89 concerns itself with those agreements; and, if so, does it concern itself in such a way as to require the royal recommendation? It seems to me, on the argument advanced so far, that the answer to the first question is no. Therefore, the answer to the second question does not apply.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, with the greatest respect-

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO ADD NEW DEFINITIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, section 4 of Bill C-73, the original act, without question empowers the minister to enter into agreements with the provinces but does not authorize the minister to enter into an agreement to pay to a province funds paid into the consolidated revenue fund. Bill C-73 did not provide that. Paragraph 9 of the model agreement the Minister of Finance filed in January says as follows:
Payments to the province: Canada hereby agrees, with respect to the aggregate amount paid to Her Majesty in right of Canada pursuant to any order made by the national administrator under sections 20 and 22 of the federal act against a person in the provincial public sector, to pay to the province an amount equal to such part of that amount as may be determined on the basis of a formula to be agreed upon between Canada and the province.
I referred to that paragraph of the model agreement last Friday. Under section 20 of Bill C-73, the administrator is to make orders directing those payments to the government of Canada. I am referring to payments referred to in paragraph 9 of the model agreement. But, Mr. Speaker, Bill C-89 amends section 20. Actually, it deletes whole sections which refer to those orders and it substitutes new sections. Those are to be the orders under which moneys are paid into the coffers of the government of Canada. Therefore, if money is to be paid in under Bill C-89 because that will be the applicable law, the money will be paid into the coffers of the government of Canada in accordance with the terms of the amended sections of the act which will be in force after the passage of Bill C-89. Surely there cannot be any payment out unless there is authority.
Bill C-89 goes to the very heart of Bill C-73 in amending the powers of the administrator. Once this bill passes, if it does pass, the administrator's orders will be governed by the amendments the House is now considering. They will be governed by the provisions of Bill C-89, not of Bill C-73. With the greatest respect, I cannot see how there can be any argument that Bill C-89 is tied integrally to Bill C-73. I do not see how any payment to a province of moneys paid under an order made pursuant to the provisions of the bill now before the House would not require the royal recommendation.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO ADD NEW DEFINITIONS
speechtext: Order, please. Before I call on the Minister of Finance, may I say this. It seems to me that the hon. member for Edmonton West says that any bill which seeks to amend a statute which was accompanied by a royal recommendation must also be accompanied by a royal recommendation whether or not it amends those provisions of the original statute which required the royal recommendation.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO ADD NEW DEFINITIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, no, with respect.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Finance):
subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO ADD NEW DEFINITIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is no argument as to whether or not both Bill C-73 and Bill C-89 authorize any payments out of the consolidated revenue fund for the purposes contained in the agreement. The provisions of both Bill C-73 and Bill C-89 would authorize payment into the consolidated revenue fund of funds which might be assessed against some person as a result of a provincial, public sector agreement. That would authorize payment into the consolidated revenue fund but not out. The critical point to be understood is this: the agreement with Ontario or the other provinces

referred to by the hon. gentleman do not purport to be agreements to pay out to the provinces. At this point there is no appropriation of funds for that purpose. The agreements are merely agreements to enter into negotiations for establishing a formula which might be followed if any payments of this kind are to be shared with a province. In other words, it is an agreement to enter into an agreement.
Various things would need to happen if there were such negotiations. If the administrator ordered payments to be made into the consolidated revenue fund, and if there were negotiations between the government of Ontario and the government of Canada about the division of such payments, then I, as Minister of Finance, would have to bring before parliament an appropriation act to appropriate such part of the consolidated revenue fund as might be necessary to cover the payment. In other words, I would have to bring forward legislation with the imprimatur of the royal recommendation in order to make such payment out. As you said, Mr. Speaker, neither Bill C-73 nor Bill C-89 authorize such payments out. Indeed, the agreement itself is only an undertaking to enter into discussions to negotiate such a formula if such a payment should be made.
On the broader basis, this seems to me the sensible way of going about it. Obviously, a considerable process of negotiation will need to be embarked upon. Until we know what the amount is to be, it makes no sense to bring in an appropriation bill in advance.

speechtext:
Order, please. During the weekend I tried to consider carefully the argument advanced by the hon. member for Edmonton West. I gave him an opportunity to clarify today and I questioned him today about the matter of primary concern to the Chair. During the weekend I examined the sections to which the hon. member for Edmonton West referred and read them today as he was referring to them. The question the Chair must decide is much less complicated than the questions which have been raised in argument, and it is this: When does a bill which comes before the House require a royal recommendation? A royal recommendation is required when the government seeks to introduce a statute which would provide the government with power to draw upon the revenues. I must find that the provisions of any statute, with respect to which it is argued that the royal recommendation is necessary, contain that possibility.
I have examined carefully Bill C-89 which proposes to amend Bill C-73 and listened carefully to the arguments advanced by the hon. member for Edmonton West. I do not see, in the bills referred to, that kind of power which would reside in the government as a result of passage of the statute. Whether or not it would reside in Bill C-89 is an argument which should have been raised in the past.
Whether or not the model agreement tabled and referred to by the hon. member for Edmonton West is an agreement without statutory authority is another matter. It is an interesting and valuable argument. But there are other remedies. That argument is not, essentially, an attack on Bill C-89. It may be an attack on the government's position
March 29, 1976

and authority vis-a-vis that particular agreement or its power to enter into an agreement specifically with a province along the lines of the model agreement.
If I may speak on the specific provisions of Bill C-89, I cannot find that the bill ought to be impeded at this stage by an insistence on the royal recommendation accompanying any provisions which I have been able to examine and study during the weekend. I therefore find that the bill is procedurally acceptable at this point.
I believe the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies) had the floor when this matter was last debated on Friday.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to comment on Bill C-89. I do not know whether I am out of order but I am pleased to have this opportunity because last Friday, while we heard some ten members speak on this bill, we had no opportunity to do so. I do not want to blame the Chair, but I think it is quite reasonable that we have our turn today. Besides, my colleague the member for Bellechasse was supposed to speak on Friday, but as the opportunity was not given him, I hope we shall have a few minutes to express our view today.
Again a few moments ago I heard hon. members discussing some legal points. What we understand about this matter of legality is always the same. I even heard Mr. Speaker say that even if there has been a royal recommendation, the government can do anything, it can act as it sees fit. It is the same thing when we approve a bill. We kill ourselves trying to make the bill as clear as possible and to propose better amendments. But at the end of the bill there is a small line which kills everything else and allows the minister to use the bill as he pleases. I think that this somewhat sums up this afternoon's discussion. Moreover, it is the same with all our bills. This is why I do not want to miss this opportunity, the second reading debate of Bill C-89 to amend Bill C-73 which established the Anti-Inflation Board.
Only four months after, the government feels the need to amend its Anti-Inflation Act whose lack of precision surprised everybody. Panic-stricken by the vertiginous price escalation which occurred these last three years, the best the government could do was to draft Bill C-73 in a hurry not to lose face.
Of course, it was hard for the Prime Minister after his 1974 campaign to control prices and wages. The government did not want to make a fool of itself by accepting the temporary freeze proposed by the Progressive Conservatives during the last election campaign. That is why they brought in this strange so-called control legislation which in fact only controls the workers' wages. Today, they move an amendment which does not actually change much in the incomes of wages earners. Bill C-89 will enable at least workers to appeal the decision of the AIB. In the AntiInflation Act of December 1975, only the party who felt aggrieved by a decision of the board could appeal. As the main responsibility for wages lay on the employer, the latter could appeal the commissioner's ruling. The best example is the case of the Irving workers.
Anti-Inflation Act
The board fined the paper company for signing an agreement with its employees exceeding the guidelines authorized by the board. The company welcomed the fine because that board decision allowed it to save millions of dollars in the years to come. But the workers saw their wages cut without even being able to protest, whereas this amendment would at least allow them to appeal against the AIB's rulings. In brief, if they are not satisfied with the ruling, they will at least be able to complain loudly about injustice, even though nothing will be changed, Mr. Speaker.
Now I take to witness the remarks of the Prime Minister who, following the demonstration staged by more than 15,000 CLC members on Parliament Hill on Monday, March 22, 1976, is reported to have said that it was all useless.
Labour was right in stating that, as days pass by, inequalities become ever more obvious. When the government launched its anti-inflation program last fall, everyone without exception expected a firm and universal policy. We even expected the right hon. Prime Minister to take as a basis the temporary freezing advocated by the Conservatives during the last electoral campaign.
It is true that the Liberals took a stand against freezing prices and salaries but the government could even have improved upon that freeze but it was afraid to lose face among its own supporters. That is why it could not afford to be realistic. So, finally, it gave birth to this partial freezing, which is so partial indeed that it cannot even be considered as such except by the wage earners.
If the government had been in earnest, it would have, first of all, controlled its own expenses by freezing its own budget. I think this is the first control which was expected in Canada: the freezing of the federal government's budget.
Some will say that expenditures had to be increased in certain areas. Yes, in certain areas, but that is precisely what is rediculous, Mr. Speaker. The expenditures in some of those areas have been reduced, for example, medicare assistance to the provinces. Expenditures have been reduced in essential areas and increased in areas where they never should have been. For instance, I have already mentioned in the House the millions of dollars appropriated by the federal government for the opening or the construction of new income tax offices in every area so as to increase the number of inspectors who will check up on everyone in order to collect income tax or other charges. The government is ready to vote millions of dollars to harass people and to take what little is left of their savings.
When I say that expenditures in some areas should have been frozen, this is one where they should have been frozen until the economy recovers. I believe that we could have kept income tax collectors in their present offices. They have quite enough room to check on every workers. Let nobody tell me that this is to serve the people better, Mr. Speaker. They want to spy on the people and check into the family budget. Today the government starts by accepting a budgetary increase of 20 per cent while asking the workers to limit themselves to an increase of 10 per cent the first year, 8 per cent the second year and 6 per cent the third year. The government is well aware that the

March 29, 1976
Anti-Inflation Act
inflation rate will be above 12 per cent in 1976, but it is still freezing the salary increase of the small wage-earner at 10 per cent. No wonder therefore if today the whole labour movement is waging an open war against the anti-inflation legislation.
In fact, the unions are not against a complete and temporary freeze of government revenue and expenditures, and even a wage freeze, provided that the freeze be universal and in discriminate. Then, the government should sit down with representatives of the federal and the provincial governments, representatives of the employers and of the employees, and look fully into the situation together in order to find a solution.
Mr. Speaker, this would be acting in a realistic way, as should be the case toward other groups and other men. People are made to discuss and not to fight each other all year round. We will not revive our national economy if we stand apart and hold our neighbour as an enemy. This is no longer the time to behave as champions and play the political game for one's group's sake. Sure enough, the easiest way for the government to rule is to create division among the groups, to provoke national and international strifes, disputes between the provinces, the groups, the blue and white-collar workers, and to make everybody stand up against each other so that it can rule as a master.
That is how we are governed today. Mr. Speaker, if the government does not finally give serious thought to the security and welfare of the entire population, then the disastrous situation we know today will persist. Although all this wrangling, all those fights were politically useful to the government by maintaining it in power, I think it would be dishonest to keep up this masquerade any longer.
And I agree with the unions when they say that the present government has a double standard policy, that we are heading towards authoritarianism, for this may be how a dictator rules. It seems to me that this may be the new society we hear so much about these days, the new society advocated everywhere.
And in support of my comments, Mr. Speaker, here is an excerpt from the CLC brief to the government concerning the government's double standard policy. I quote Le Devoir of March 23:
When a union has managed in its last agreement to keep ahead of the consumer price index and secure for its members a 2 per cent productivity premium, those grains can be cancelled in the new agreement by the so-called experience adjustment factor. On the other hand, a corporation which has made excessive profits during the five years prior to October 14, 1975 is allowed to maintain its profits at 95 per cent of that level. There is no experience adjustment factor in the case of profits.
If inflation exceeds the increase allowed under the guidelines for the first year, we are prevented from making up for our losses before the second year of our contract. On the other hand, any cost increase by a corporation is immediately reflected in a price increase; in other words, the corporation does as it always does.
The Anti-Inflation Act has no effect whatsoever on large corporations. And then, further down, the union members' brief says:

More than that; they policy applied through your anti-inflation program, as can be seen from what is happening and the prevailing mood, is leading our country straight down the road to authoritarianism. Act C-73 and its regulations are turning every employer into an agent responsible for imposing the will of the State upon the workers and their unions.

That is authoritarianism, Mr. Speaker. Someone on the other side said that the unions are experts in authoritarianism. I believe that, in this regard, they have the best example right here with this government. And if we are going on with this kind of dictatorship, I repeat what I said previously, we will be introducing more and more disorders in our society, and among social groups and tomorrow we will be faced with total anarchy unless the government wakes up in time.
We must hope-and I am looking forward to it with all my heart-that the government will become aware of these facts and stop being the servant of financial groups. It is a fact that it was elected by them, that it is here for them but if the government is sincere or wishes to restore the peace that everybody expects in this country, it should momentarily forget financiers and financial interests and devote itself for a while to social concerns.

Mr. Speaker, I think the House is extending, as it is difficult to see each other now. In any event, I would like to say a few words about this bill. Last Friday I wanted to make a few comments.
Mr. Speaker, once more I would like to be the spokesman for low and average income earners, such as workers in general and farmers who have irregular incomes and who too often have to operate at a loss for certain productions. When this anti-inflation policy was announced, I declared that it was impossible to support current government measures because low income earners would be most affected and big corporations would go on making profits and even too often, excessive profits. We now have the evidence which has been published in newspapers that Dominion stores' profits have risen by 28 per cent since the announcement of the anti-inflation policy, which means that unfortunately the projections I made at the time have been proven right.
I said that these measures would contribute to pertur-bate the social climate in our country. The ensuing events have shown I was right once again, as we can see by the various outbreaks of opposition that this law has provoked all across Canada. We only have to hear the sometimes violent words uttered by those who feel they are victims of these controls. I do not approve of violence nor of violent words, but when there are groups who feel their rights have not been respected and that they are being done an injustice, the violence of their reaction is understandable.
Let us have a look at the disputes which oppose the Ontario and Quebec governments to the public service employees and related categories. We see that the situation is in a state of complete disorganization which is likely to affect the students considerably: in Quebec the school year is on the verge of being a complete failure because of a dispute concerning money. In each news bulletin from my province we hear of schools which are closed, either by the school boards, or for study sessions, or because there is no more transportation or because children refuse to go to school or are going when there is no authority to let them get into the buildings. We are in a complete state of chaos. I do hope that these conditions will be corrected in any event but meanwhile, people who are concerned are worried to see the late development of these events in our country.
March 29, 1976

The Trudeau government does not deal with the cause of the evil; on the contrary, it attempts to lessen the effects of the true cause with the expectation that our corrupted economic system will survive and let the millionaire club continue to control the economic and political life of our country. I hope that such are not the objectives aimed at, but anyhow such are the results. They are rich Canadians who know that our economic system is furthering the interests of a minority of financiers despite what is suggested by some politicians who have become stooges and who quite often maintain that our economic system enables many Canadians to be affluent.
Those great characters, most of them unknown to all nevertheless rule the economic life of the country. Indeed they control our financial institutions. They steer our economy from deflation to inflation periods. In this connection, it would be beneficial to read over again the remarks of His Holiness Pope Pius XI, in his encyclical on economic and social problems published in 1931. I will quote a very interesting excerpt;
It was in 1931, but the situation remains the same in 1976.
"What first strikes us nowadays is not only the concentration of wealth but the building up of a huge power, a discretionary economic power, in the hands of a small group of men who are not usually the owners but just act as trustees and managers of the capital they administer as they wish. This power is particularly great among those who, holders and absolute masters of money, govern credit and grant it at their discretion. In so doing, they somehow distribute its blood to the economic body whose life depends on them, so that without their consent, no one can any longer breathe."
Mr. Speaker, let us ask one of these men, whose power has become greater than all the governments of Canada, how much he is worth in dollars and cents. This would amount to asking of these people to tell us in what position he prefers to make love. He surely has a preference but will not dare tell us and will then answer in the same way.
Our debt-credit system for the financing of the public sector is obsolete and constitutes one of the main causes of inflation and unemployment. That is why Bill C-89 is now before us, in an attempt to find solutions to such situations. It costs too much to this government, to provincial and municipal governments to finance public utilities. The more we go ahead, the deeper we plunge into the abyss; the more we run into debts, the more it costs to pay the interests on these public debts. The more taxes we levy, the less money the government has to do something else, to proceed with the building of piers and merchant marine vessels, and with the construction of public buildings which are needed by the people.
For instance, let us take the Jacques Cartier bridge in Montreal whose initial cost Canadians have paid up to now three times in interests alone, and the capital has still to be paid back. Let us look, in the province of Quebec, at the James Bay. This project is supposed to cost $12 billion, of which $6 billion are in interests alone. It is disgusting, Mr. Speaker, to see how money-capital is so well rewarded and how we fail to reward work-capital.
Anti-Inflation Act
Again this year, the most important item in the federal budget is the debt service: $4 billion a year in interests. If this is not inflation, I wonder when we are going to find a real example of it. Again last week, the Bank of Canada increased the bank rate from 9 to 9'A per cent, which will enable the banks to increase once more their interest rates. The burden will fall therefore on borrowers, which will result in an increase in operating costs.
And as a consequential effect, prices will rise further. In the end, once more, consumers will have to shoulder this price increase due to increased interest rates. In that regard, the government is doing nothing. I ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) whether the Governor of the Bank of Canada consulted with him last week before authorizing an increase in the discount rate of 'A per cent. If we are really serious about fighting inflation, we will have to ask each and everyone and every organization in Canada to do their share and not only ask for it, but require it. We require restraints from labour but we let the door wide open to big business, charted banks and multinationals.
According to a press report, the minister announced that he "was giving up the idea of a special tax on export profits"-I read that in La Presse and I quote:
The Federal government has just provided organized labour with a new opportunity to howl at the inequity of the anti-inflation program.
Yielding to pressures that have been building up since the program was announced last October, the Cabinet has decided not to implement its planned 100 per cent tax on part of the export profits of Canadian businesses. Instead, the Anti-Inflation Board will merely monitor the profits of export companies and the way such profits are reinvested.
In other words, export companies may, theoretically make unlimited profits on their export market transactions, without being bothered by Mr. Pepin's Board. On the other hand, their Canadian employees will not be allowed to share this manna: they will remain subject to wage controls, which are more than ever the basis of the anti-inflation program.
Those are, Mr. Speaker, two examples which show that the anti-inflation legislation and regulations are not really implemented in all fairness with repect to every Canadian, whatever his occupation in society.
With regard to the interest rate increase, the governor of the Bank of Canada has stated that it was intended to slow down the rate of growth of the money supply. The authorities of our central bank intend thus to maintain a rigid credit policy. This may surprise financial quarters who would expect, to some extent, a lowering of the rate that serves as a barometer for money rental in Canada.
Even financiers do not agree. How can one give good advice to the government on its financial policy, on its economic policy, that might ensure greater well-being of the people and allow low-income workers to upgrade their confidence not only in Canada but in the government that manages the affairs of this country?
Last week, the right hon. Prime Minister, in reply to a question I raised in the House, asked me whether the hon. member had a formula that would enable the government to finance the public sector more adequately. I took good note of his question and I want to advise him that there is a formula which, to my mind, would deserve to be tried out and which certainly could not give worse results than the ones that are advocated and applied by this government.

Anti-Inflation Act
Mr. Speaker, there is a way the government can raise the standard of living of all Canadians, without increasing anything at all, without taking anything from anyone, without paralyzing the economy, without bringing about inflation or deflation. And that would be to have public capital financed by means of interest-free credit advances, issued by the bank that belongs to all Canadians, known as the Bank of Canada. The government would now have a wonderful opportunity of applying that policy and I mean with regard to the construction of the building at the corner of Wellington and Bank that will house the offices of the Bank of Canada.
This will be quite an experience; it is so close to this Parliament and so if the experience is successful, as I am convinced it will be, all hon. members will have a chance to visit our bank, our institution in our own building, paid by us and not financed by New York financiers, who are leading New York City to bankruptcy.
Such a measure would result in lower taxes, those taxes which the government collects to pay the interest on the public debt or the borrowings he makes, and would correspondingly increase the money supply available to consumers to buy the goods they need. Although it is true that Social Crediters do not find much support for their ideas on the setting up of a national dividend or a minimum guaranteed annual income, some people on the other hand are in favour of the creation of new interest-free credit to finance public capital.
An economist named Theobald considered this problem of government financing. He came to the conclusion arrived at by the members of the Social Credit Party a long time ago, namely the financing of public capital through new interest-free credits. This economist goes on to say, and I quote:
A government has three methods of obtaining the funds necessary to meet its obligations. First they can tax the people and the institutions to get possession of their money...
-this is the method used in Canada-
... Secondly, they can borrow money from the people and the institutions and pay interest on the borrowings. Thirdly, they can simply create money and use the funds created for their purchases.
This is the formula we advocate for public financing of long-term capital expenditures. I continue:
One thing everybody agreed on in the years 1936 was that the government should never create money. This opposition to the creation of money was based on the belief that the demand for goods should always equal supply as long as the government did not interfere with economy. Another economist, Keynes, destroyed this belief by demonstrating that demand and supply were not necessarily always equal in wealthy countries.
Keynes, the economist, inspired many governments in the last years.
There are several methods to fill the gap between supply and demand. It would be possible, Mr. Speaker, to lower the supply level without affecting materially the demand by paying the same salary for shorter hours. It would then be possible to increase the demand by telling the people that more gooods are necessary for a decent life and a better standard of living.

This government could simply fill the gap between the actual and potential production by building wharves, clearing slums, controlling pollution because untapped ressources would be found in the economy. The government would not have to raise its revenues through taxes and borrowings; money could be simply created out of additional funds without imposing any inflation since, by definition, there would be no shortage of goods.
This is, Mr. Speaker, the testimony of American economist Robert Theobald who thinks it is possible to democratize money and use new interest-free credits for the development and capital goods of our country. To this end, I suggest that the government use the Anti-Inflation Board to educate the people on the government financing system and see to it to make everyone understand the simple facts and the functions of money, whether it be coins, paper money or bank credits under various forms.
This does not mean that endless studies on economic and monetary policies are absolutely necessary; it means that everybody should be able to understand, first, that money is a means of exchange, a payment method in itself: it is without any value and does not cost anything. Intrinsically, it has no value at all. Second, the control and regularization of the volume of money required must be materially improved to meet the needs of modern progress and of change due to an economy of capitalization.
In the past few years, there are projects under way with a view to improving energy resources, extending the heritage, improving shipping and port facilities, and finally all public utilities needed by the Canadian people. All these projects would become important assets for society and would furthermore create a great number of jobs. These projects would cost hundreds of million dollars, but it would be less than nothing compared to the advantages for the Canadian people. It would be applying, I think, Keynes' theory who advocated so strongly the fact of making financially possible what is physically workable.
But in order to do so, we should set up a national credit bureau which would provide the necessary funds for the production of goods and services which would benefit the whole of society. This would create jobs as long as natural ressources remain plentiful. In a peace time free society the over supply of labour cannot be forced into various occupations but with education, retraining, good wages and proper housing, it can be enticed into accepting other jobs. We must remember that the gross national product can and should be increased if we wish to ensure a reasonable standard of living for all Canadians.
Never before, Mr. Speaker, has our ability to produce, to move and to communicate been as great as it is now, yet this government's demands and requests that we tighten our belts are inevitably conducive to controls that producers impose on themselves in various ways. Let us consider, for instance, the case of the dairy producers who must necessarily decrease their production if they do not want to be penalized.
As a matter of fact, representations were made today asking the government to take steps to prevent that their annual revenues be decreased by 19 per cent compared with last year's. All those Canadians who participated today in the demonstration on Parliament Hill do not ask
March 29, 1976

for the impossible, they only want that justice be done. They do not want charity.
If the government in its wisdom decides before Wednesday to reduce the production quotas of industrial milk producers, it has in turn to increase the subsidies to allow them to get at least the same revenue as last year's. Generally the government's anti-inflation legislation provides for a 10 per cent increase in the wage earners' revenues and, as regards this group of Canadians called industrial milk producers, if the policy is not improved within two days, those producers will suffer, in 1976-77, a decrease of about 19 per cent in their revenues.
Those figures are proven by accurate calculations of production costs, operation costs, sale prices and revenues that may be obtained by the operators. I therefore believe the government should show some of its teeth to those neglecting to pay their taxes. The Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cullen) recently answered a question under my name on the Order Paper. He informed us that multinational and national corporations had income tax arrears in the order of $223 million as of March 31, 1975, on which they pay 6 per cent interest. There is no mention of whether they pay a penalty as do private taxpayers who are penalized for late filing. And if income tax officers in the Department of National Revenue so decide, because they have every power, even under Section 152 (7) of the Income Tax Act which provides, and this I checked once more yesterday to answer a taxpayer, even when returns are filed in time, even if the taxpayer acted in good faith; if the tax officer decides not to accept his figures and assess him as he is empowered by the act, the statute allows them to blow hot and cold. I feel this is utterly unfair.
I would urge the government to show some firmness in respect of those big corporations neglecting to pay their taxes in time, and give part of the taxes so recouped to the Canadian Milk Board so that industrial milk producers may remain in business and hope to go on serving the people of Canada. I feel that within two days the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) together with his colleague the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) and other members of cabinet should review that policy, in all fairness to industrial milk producers. I believe it is in the interest of every Canadian that the policy be more adequate and take into better account the representations by industrial milk producers.
For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I feel Bill C-89 does not include many significant improvements to the Anti-Inflation Act. True, some provision was made for appeal in certain circumstances, but basically the large organizations will still be all powerful. They will go on doing as they wish, because clearly accounting procedures give them all kinds of legal ways to come down with balance sheets that fill their needs and allow them to go around the act, to make more profits notwithstanding anti-inflation legislation such as the one passed in Parliament in December.
I hope the government will take heed of representations by hon. members in this House. I realize that my representations on behalf of low or middle income people have probably less weight than those made by persons contributing generously to election funds, but nevertheless I
Quarantine Act
think it is my duty and that of all hon. members to stand for something which, in my opinion is a just cause.
And if after a while we realize that these people take advantage of their representives or of the situation, it would still be time to come up with another law to bring them back to their senses. But so far I admit that this Anti-Inflation Act does not treat fairly low income earners and does not provide sufficient enforcement to make large commercial organizations or big corporations realize that we in this country are faced with a crucial issue which we must straighten out all together, that is inflation.
If we succeed in putting our economy back on its feet, I hope we shall be able to allow our workers, the labour force of Canada, to work and earn a living. If the government and the cabinet really want to fight inflation, we shall have to use a lot of money to put everyone to work, to increase our gross national product so that we may say in the very near future: The gross national product has increased, unemployment is down. If we can really say those things honestly, we shall be able to say that we have done something to fight inflation, money will once more play its true role and the dollar will regain its real value.
However I am convinced-and I would like to be wrong-that the action we are taking to try to fight the problems caused by an unbalanced economic and financial system will not succeed in meeting this objective because it does not go at the root of the problem. This is the monetary system, milk which is in the hands of private agencies which exploit this system as if it were a commodity instead of using it like a service. This is the difference. A monetary system is a service and not a commodity. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I close by asking once again that something effective be done in the next two days to help industrial milk producers in Canada.
Is the House ready for the question? Is it the pleasure of the House to adopt the said motion?
