subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND APPLICATION TO DANGEROUS DISEASES
speechtext:
that Bill S-31, to amend the Quarantine
21804-I3'/2

March 29, 1976
Quarantine Act
Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I would like today to move second reading of Bill S-31, an Act to amend the Quarantine Act. The intent of the substantive amendments proposed is to provide the legislative authority for prompt and appropriate action at Canadian ports of entry to prevent the importation into Canada of dangerous diseases in addition to the four infectious and contagious diseases named in the Schedule to the Quarantine Act.
The Quarantine Act is at present contained in Chapter 33, 1st supplement, of the Revised Statutes of Canada and was proclaimed in force on January 1, 1972. The act of 1972 was then a recasting of the original Quarantine Act which had been in effect for over one hundred years. Indeed, the orginal act was passed in the very first session of the Canadian Parliament in 1868, and, except for two amendments introduced in 1918 and 1919, remained in force until the 1972 revision.
There is an old proverb that goes: "There are three things done well in haste: flying from the plague, escaping quarrels and catching flies". A strange combination, but undoubtedly words of wisdom in their days. However, social medicine has made tremendous advances and we no longer deal with a plague by fleeing, but rather try to contain it and prevent it from spreading to new areas.
In the early nineteenth century in London, for example, cholera would periodically be brought in by travellers from abroad and a fresh epidemic started. This situation could have been prevented by effective quarantine laws. The concept of quarantine is not new however. The word "quarantine" dates back to at least the 14th century and was ascribed to that 40 days of isolation imposed by the local government on travellers arriving in certain European ports in an attempt to prevent them from infecting the local inhabitants. The proposed amendments, however, do not prescribe a period of isolation as drastic as 40 days.
The present Quarantine Act is designed to minimize the risk of importation into Canada of the four major quaran-tinable diseases. At the time of the last revision of the act these major diseases of concern were smallpox, cholera, yellow fever and plague, all highly contagious and infectious diseases. Fortunately, these diseases have been eradicated in Canada.
Great improvements in global health have unquestionably resulted from preventive health measures applied in Canada and in other countries throughout the world. For example, smallpox, I am glad to say, appears to have been all but wiped out. The latest bulletin on the subject issued by the World Health Organization shows the existence of only 61 reported cases, confined to one small area of the world, of this once dreaded disease. However, until major quarantinable diseases completely disappear from the world, legislation which provides the authority to inspect, examine and, if necessary detain, international passengers and international carriers entering Canada must be retained. This is particularly true in the light of the present jet age, when high capacity aircraft can transport over 400 people to Canada from any corner of the globe within a single day. As I mentioned, the present legislation provides Canada with quarantine powers only in respect to

the four scheduled diseases-cholera, plague, smallpox and yellow fever.
The diseases-and only these diseases-are recognized by the World Health Organization as requiring quarantine control. Through its adherence to the International Health Regulations, Canada has quarantine control only over these four infectious diseases.
The present act is quite specific with regard to the four scheduled diseases and measures are currently being taken to safeguard Canadians against them. For example, quarantine stations have been designated at all major ports of entry and at the present time, there are 17 of these across Canada. Of this number, six relate to maritime traffic and the remaining 11 to air traffic. However, recent international experience and new developments have demonstrated that a vacuum exists in the present act. New and highly communicable diseases, such as Lassa fever and Marburg virus disease, have appeared in some countries.

It may be recalled that last December, in response to a question from the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Rynard) I mentioned that I proposed to introduce into the House during the current session a number of changes to the Quarantine Act. These changes are now before the House and are intended to deal with such dangerous exotic diseases as Lassa fever.
A few words about this disease might help to put things into perspective. Lassa fever was first recognized after two American missionary nurses died of a mysterious, undiagnosed illness, in the town of Lassa in northeastern Nigeria, in 1969. Subsequent laboratory investigations revealed that Lassa was a dangerous, acute, infectious disease caused by a virus which was isolated, incidentally, only about six years ago. There is evidence to suggest that the disease is not actually new, but that it has been indigenous to certain countries in West Africa for many years. It is, however, only since 1969 that it has been recognized by specific, medically accepted nomenclature. Subsequent outbreaks of the disease in West Africa have confirmed its very high mortality rate.
It is the tendency for the virus to be passed from person to person and the concern that it could be spread across continents by rats carrying the virus that makes the disease so potentially dangerous in the world. This fact, along with the increase in the speed, volume and worldwide scope of international travel, results in a potential threat to Canadian public health. Approximately 40 million travellers pass through Canadian ports of entry annually. Should any one of these be a carrier of a new or heretofore unknown dangerous disease, there is not sufficient provision for emergency authority in the act at present to detain or isolate that person, even if the disease is confirmed as presenting a grave danger to public health. Authority does exist in the present act to permit quarantine control of diseases other than the four now listed in the schedule, but only through the passage of an order in council adding the new disease to the schedule.
Our problem with the provisions of this section is twofold. In the first instance, addition to the schedule of, for example, Lassa fever as a disease subject to regular quarantine control would not accord with Canada's obligations under the international health regulations. I mentioned
March 29, 1976

earlier that the four diseases listed at present were the only ones currently recognized by the World Health Organization as being subject to the international health regulations. These regulations stipulate that adequate control of these diseases justifies appropriate routine quarantine action being taken by signatory countries, of which Canada is one, with no reservations.
I have used Lassa fever as an example of the type of disease that is causing some concern, but the same situation applies to other dangerous diseases both known and, as yet, unknown. It is obviously impossible, in advance of an emergency, to list a disease that, while widely accepted as highly dangerous, has not yet achieved international identification nor consensus as to its medical name.
It is, therefore, necessary to honour the international protocol while at the same time providing the means whereby, during an emergency, quarantine control can be exercised over all-and I repeat, all-dangerous diseases. If a dangerous disease does enter Canada, that disease will be added to the schedule by means of an order in council and will remain on the schedule until the danger has passed. Thus, the disease in question will not-I repeat, will not- be subject to routine or regular quarantine control, but merely to emergency control for a limited period.
This leads, naturally, to the second problem which is one of time. There is simply not enough time between the appearance at a port of entry of a new suspect disease and the passage of an order in council to ensure that appropriate protective measures can be taken. Immediate detention and isolation is imperative in such cases; thus, the method provided for in the present act is obviously inadequate for the purpose of meeting such an emergency. What this bill before us will do is allow immediate detention of persons suspected or known to have a dangerous disease which is not on the schedule until measures are taken to add that disease to the schedule. Again I emphasize that this would be an emergency control for a limited period only.
Other countries, such as the United States and Great Britain, have had for several years emergency quarantine powers for diseases other than the four recognized by the international health regulations. It is, in effect, similar emergency powers that are now being proposed for Canada but with the added provision for judicial review of any detentions ordered in such circumstances.
What, specifically, is being proposed, Mr. Speaker, are two major changes. The first is to ensure a means within the provisions of the Quarantine Act whereby a quarantine officer at a port of entry may, in an emergency situation and with the approval of the Minister of National Health and Welfare, order the dentention of a person arriving in Canada whom that quarantine officer reasonably believes to be the carrier, or to have been recently in close proximity to a carrier, of a contagious or infectious disease not listed in the schedule to the act.
Such unlisted diseases are referred to as "other diseases" and are, intentionally, not listed in a separate schedule to the act in order to provide needed flexibility. This detention will be for a period of time not to exceed 14 days. An important feature of the amendment is the reflection of the government's concern that the Canadian Bill of Rights be
Quarantine Act
fully respected in any detention so ordered. Proposed subsection 8.1(6) makes it necessary for the Minister of National Health and Welfare to justify, within 48 hours, the detention order to a judge of the superior court of the province in which the person is detained. In such instances, the judge is required to hear the case within one day and is empowered to revoke, vary or confirm the detention order.
The second major change would provide for detention in those cases where it is definitely determined, as opposed to being suspected, by a quarantine officer that a person arriving in Canada has a disease considered dangerous to public health. Detention in these circumstances would, again, require ministerial approval.
In addition to the two major amending clauses that I have outlined, there are six further amendments the purpose of which is either to clarify the existing act or to make changes consequential to the substantive amendments.

Before concluding, Mr. Speaker, I should like to make it clear that the proposed amendments before us now form just a part of the overall contingency provisions which are being developed and revised on a continuing basis. For example, in response to the December question from the hon. member from Simcoe North, I also mentioned that a working group had been formed to look into isolation facilities. Because the interest of provinces in the provision of adequate isolation accomodation at strategic locations across Canada parallels that of the federal government, the participation by provincial officials is an important aspect of the discussions of the working group. Recommendations can be expected from these discussions on the type of facility needed to treat the most virulent of diseases.
To summarize, Mr. Speaker, the amendments proposed are both logical and essential if all due precautions are to continue to be taken to preserve the health of Canadians- particularly in the light of ever changing world conditions. I expect and hope the bill under discussion will be regarded as akin to insurance protection against a potential threat but, like many such contingency provisions, will be rarely if ever utilized.
For example, under the present act, there have been no involuntary detentions within the last 15 years, though, of course, there have been routine medical checks performed on ships and planes a number of times.

In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank hon. members opposite for their agreement to proceed with the speedy consideration of this bill.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND APPLICATION TO DANGEROUS DISEASES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the beginning of my remarks I wish to say we do not have any intention of trying to block this bill. We do, however, have a number of reservations to express because this bill will not only affect visitors to this country in the near future but in fact will become permanent legislation affecting all Canadians who come and go from this country.
It was interesting to note the minister indicated that the first Quarantine Act was passed in 1868. That act, which was introduced by the Conservative government of the

March 29, 1976
Quarantine Act
day, lasted for 50 years. The government at that time had so much foresight that no changes were required for a period of 50 years, as opposed to the present administration which passed some amendments four years ago, in 1972, which are now no longer adequate. I think this is a clear indication of the type of legislation lacking in foresight which the present government might bring forward.
One thing that has concerned me somewhat during the past week or so is the great degree of pressure applied on this side of the House by the other side to try to shoot this bill through the House as quickly as a bullet would go past one's nose. I do not like passing, with such haste, bills which have such far reaching results. In addition, we as an opposition party have an obligation to the people of Canada to ensure that anything that passes this House with such haste is not legislation which in some way may be harmful to the country. We are very much interested in seeing good laws passed through this chamber and we must ensure that all the facts are on the table before passage is approved.
One suggestion I heard as a reason for this bill-I am sorry the minister did not refer to it-is the fact that we will be hosting the Olympics in the summer of 1976; and we need this bill to take appropriate precautions. But the minister chose to talk about Lassa fever instead. We know Lassa fever has been around for some time-even before the last changes were made to the Quarantine Act. The minister did not indicate whether the Olympics had anything to do with the desire to speed though parliament legislation, or whether it would make any difference in terms of how we receive Olympic athletes from areas where these exotic diseases exist or from areas where other diseases not mentioned in the Quarantine Act might exist. Perhaps the minister could clarify this matter, as the point is significant.
The minister suggested that we must pass this bill in order to control the spread in this country of Lassa fever and other virus fevers, including those at present unknown diseases which may come up in the future. He shows commendable farsightedness in the concern about diseases yet unknown. Perhaps this bill will fare better than the previous bill passed in 1972 which was in force only four years. This one may be in force longer, as it covers diseases known and yet unknown.
The minister is asking for far reaching quarantine powers to be extended to himself and his officials. Before we grant such far reaching powers we must make sure they are needed. Under the provisions of this bill, athletes coming to this country from West Africa or Europe, and Canadians who have been visiting those areas, could be quarantined for lengthy periods. Therefore, we should know specifically to what use he will put the powers the minister seeks. The bill does not specify how these powers are to be used and is, therefore, deficient in that regard. As this bill will affect people so directly, it would be useful if we could see the regulations which will be in force under this law before we pass the bill so that we may know exactly what we are passing.
We do not yet know how widespread Lassa fever is. According to some authorities, only about 100 cases have

been confirmed, world wide. I am told that there could be many more unconfirmed cases. Perhaps we are over-reacting to a potential threat to Canadians which is very small. That is how it seems at first glance. Appearing before the standing committee of the other place when this bill was being considered there, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare said recently, in 1976, that the World Health Organization had rejected an application Canada had made two years earlier to have Lassa fever added to the list of notifiable major quaranti-nable diseases. The parliamentary secretary said:
The application was rejected on the grounds that not enough was known at that time about the disease, and that it was doubtful that including Lassa fever in the international health regulations would be effective in controlling the spread of the disease.
Since the World Health Organization obviously has not changed its mind about the utility of listing Lassa fever among quarantinable diseases and since Lassa fever is the only disease to which the amendments to the Quarantine Act might apply, it is fair to ask if there is any point to this bill at all. The members of the World Health Organization are experts possessed of information. If they question the inclusion of the disease in the list of quarantinable diseases and our present methods of controlling the spread of the disease, should we not examine the matter further?
In short, although the bill, ostensibly, is designed to control the spread of diseases like Lassa fever and the Marburg virus, it does not mention them specifically. Why not? Is the minister afraid of international repercussions? Does he think that some countries, particularly West African countries, those sending Olympic athletes to this country, will accuse us of detaining their citizens under the pretext that we are controlling the spread of Lassa fever in this country? If the government wants to avoid such accusations, it should be more frank about the intent of the bill, and we could deal with this matter more easily.
The minister referred several times to it, as do the explanatory notes to the bill, that these extraordinary powers are needed to deal with emergency situations. So far, no one has defined such emergencies or what action is contemplated in these emergency situations. This omission raises questions about the minister's sincerity in dealing with this question. He ought to tell the House what emergencies the government has in mind and how the government proposes to deal with them. In the past, the quarantine officer made decisions regarding quarantine. This made sense, as quarantine officers were either physicians or nurses working under the direction of a physician. The minister proposes a different approach. Apparently he does not trust physicians to make the right decision: he, himself, wants that authority. Why does the minister want this authority? Why is he taking this power away from physicians who are trained experts in the field and can be relied on to make the right decision? He ought to explain that matter as well.
Health authorities agree that it is difficult to intercept carriers of quarantinable disease at their point of entry to this country. It is almost impossible to do this, as 40 million travellers cross our borders every year. I do not see how this bill will be effective in preventing the entry to this country of carriers of disease. In today's world of rapid travel, an infected disease carrier can travel from foreign parts to Canada very quickly. Hence, would it not be better
March 29, 1976

not to insist on controls at the border and to insist on more stringent examination of travellers coming from areas of known infection or in which disease is endemic? The minister suggests that we will tighten border controls. He did not refer to more stringent physical examination of people coming from areas rife with infection or where disease may be endemic. He did not indicate what kind of authority will be given to officials at the ports of entry, or specifically how they are going to detain people. It comes back to the same thing: under normal circumstances we have 40 million travellers coming through our ports of entry and with the Olympics there will perhaps be a few million more.
If the minister is concerned about Lassa fever it would be logical for him to instruct the quarantine officers specifically to watch for and perhaps even require people coming from areas in West Africa, where this disease exists, to be examined. If he is concerned about Marburg virus fever, perhaps he should look at the possibility of examining people from those areas, the athletes and indeed the fans coming to watch the athletes in action. Perhaps they, too, should be examined at the ports of entry. However, the minister does not say they are going to do that. We are left in a complete vacuum as to what the government will be doing. Greater powers are being asked for without our being told how they will be used.
The minister also indicated there were some 17 quarantine stations in the country-six maritime stations and 11 air stations. I have a document before me entitled "The Canadian contingency plan for Lassa fever" which states that at this time there are no safe facilities in Canada for isolation of patients or for the protection of attending staff and the avoidance of laboratory bio-hazards from this disease.
The minister has not told us what he is going to do about that. It is fine to isolate them, but the fact is we do not appear to have safe facilities in which to isolate them; by that I mean safe from the point of view of spreading the disease to people who work in the quarantine area. If it is a laboratory which will have to be involved in confirming what the disease is in fact, we do not have laboratories that are sufficiently safe to protect the laboratory workers from the disease in any of these 17 areas to which the minister referred. He has not given us any assurance that we can indeed handle these isolation cases with safety as far as our own workers are concerned. On page 5 it is said that the existing facilities admittedly do not meet bio-hazard safety standards in dealing with such dangerous communicable diseases, and a definitive contingency plan for Canada must await the availability of a purpose-designed isolation facility and maximum security laboratory.
It sounds from that as though the contingency plan with which we are now dealing is perhaps a little premature. We do not have the kind of designed isolation facilities which are secure, medically speaking, that are required.
With those comments and reservations, I again ask the minister to give us answers to these questions and inform us before trying to ram this bill through committee. We will, of course, object to any attempt to ram it through the committee. We will insist upon hearing a number of wit-
Adjournment Motion
nesses whom we believe are experts in this area, in addition to the experts provided by the minister's department.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND APPLICATION TO DANGEROUS DISEASES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, both the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) and the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk) have made reference to the history of this legislation; therefore, I need not say anything in that respect.
It is interesting to note that we are dealing with an act that has been on the statute books of Canada, in one way or another, since the year one. Even though it has not been amended very many times during a century or more, it is understandable that in these days of new diseases and new viruses, coupled with the speed of transportation, a new look at our quarantine provisions could well be necessary. Speaking generally, we concede the need for this legislation. Although there are questions we may want to ask when the bill gets to committee, we are prepared to give it our support.
Like the previous speaker and his colleagues, when this bill was put into our hands one of the first approaches we made to it was from the standpoint of civil liberties. We wanted to know whether any rights, either of Canadians going abroad and coming back home or of visitors or immigrants to this country, were being set aside.
As I say, we have looked at the bill rather critically from that point of view. I must say that we do not see it as a curtailment or denial of civil liberties. Canadians are not, by this bill, being denied the right to come back to Canada. Immigrants or visitors are not, by this bill, being denied the right to come into this country if they qualify under the Immigration Act, and so on. What is being done is that if persons are suspected, not only of the four diseases that are already listed but of new diseases whether known or unknown, they will be subject to quarantine for a time equal to the incubation period of that disease, or sent to their destination under certain agreements to meet with medical authorities, and so on. On that basis we do not see it as an interference with civil liberties.
I had hoped that I might be able to finish before five o'clock. However, I will need another four or five minutes. Therefore, I had better call it five o'clock.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED FEDERAL GOVERNMENT CONSIDERATION OF COMPREHENSIVE PLAN OF DECENTRALIZED GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider a comprehensive plan of decentralization, as envisioned by the Special Joint Committee of the Senate and House of Commons on the Constitution of Canada, with special emphasis on, (a) the constitutional division powers, (b) decentralizing the decision-making process within federal government departments, (c) improved intergovernmental relations.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in conclusion-I have found this a good way to begin a speech-decentralization may not be a glamorous word but it is one of the most important words in the political lexicon today. In its fullness, it provides a bold, exciting new way to restore the vitality of Canada. For it is through decentralization that the country can be pulled back from overdependency on federal government officials and Canadians across the land provided with a way to develop their opportunities.
I hope to show why, and how, the federal government ought to press vigorously a decentralization policy in a way that will enable municipalities today to cope with the explosion of social problems brought about by urbanization. Before long in this debate a government spokesman will be telling us that the federal government is already committed to decentralization. Actually, the present policies of the federal government make decentralization a game of musical chairs adding to the proliferation of government. I am arguing here that decentralization, first of all, depends upon a determination to slow down and control the haphazard growth of government in Canada.
This goal is all the more important when we grasp the implication of two basic trends in Canada: first, government spending now accounts for 40 per cent of the gross
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. McCleave).]
national product; second, 19 per cent of Canada's work force, two million people, are on the public payroll. What this means is that government at all levels is growing faster than the economy. The Economic Council of Canada has warned us about this escalation. Unless it is slowed, the spending of the three levels of government will exceed 50 per cent of the GNP before the end of this decade. Provincial expenditures are rising fastest of all. This is principally because of delivery programs in the social security area which are direct offshoots of the state of the economy and the federal government's economic and social policies.
The trend toward a dominantly governmental economy is now a chief characteristic of our society. That trend must be broken, because the increasing intervention of the state in economic and social life will substantially change-for the worse-the character of our society. Increasing tax burdens on private economic activity will inevitably lead to the elimination of that activity, and the increasing dependency of people on government programs will result in diminished initiative in the much-needed further development of Canada.
Around the world people are asking: Can democracy cope with the complex problems of a modern, interdependent global community? There is a "crisis of political faith" in the ability of democratic governments to respond, according to the distinguished social scientist, Robert Heil-broner-"All the polls indicate a serious dropping off of public belief in the efficacy and trustworthiness of government." Canada is by no means exempt from this voter disenchantment. Distrust of a large, powerful and faceless bureaucracy in Ottawa is intensifying. People are paying higher taxes than ever to support an ever-growing government-and yet the problems of transportation, housing and safety in society are getting worse. Decentralization is not a magic answer to all this, but without decentralization the problems of the municipalities, the level of government closest to the people, will become chaotic.
The rate of urbanization is nothing short of a phenomenon. Before the end of this century, 94 per cent of Canadians will be urbanized and three-quarters will live in 12 major cities. Urbanization is caused by an interlocking set of developments spawned by exploding technology. Government efforts must be directed toward managing the process of urbanization. The special problems of urbanization-public assistance, transportation, environmental management, leisure, recreation and housing-interact on one another and demand more money which municipalities have no way of raising, thus exacerbating their dependence on provincial and federal government grants.
The quality of life in urban centres is diminishing, despite local efforts; the institutional framework of government was established long before the social impact of urbanization was ever dreamed of. As the role and level of government in Canada has expanded, each level-federal, provincial and municipal-has become involved in areas in which the other levels previously had a special or exclusive interest. Complexity and fragmentation of government has followed. This has resulted in a proliferation of duplicative, autonomy-seeking special agencies in each level of government and hence has highlighted the problem of a decision-making mechanism which can no longer respond
March 29, 1976

to the needs of a society in an era of accelerating social change.
Thus, a new philosophy at the top is needed to meet the super problems of big government and urbanization. Only a new philosophy can counter the mounting evidence that government is big, rather than strong; flabby, rather than powerful-that it costs a great deal and doesn't achieve very much. More tinkering with government will not be enough. That is why the present federal government's policies on decentralization are inadequate. They are focused on spreading out certain government departments such as DREE, Revenue, and Supply and Services, and diversifying the sources of federal purchasing, as the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien) said on September 3, 1975, when he announced a task force on decentralization of government. This approach is too narrow a concept of decentralization. A comprehensive plan based on a philosophy of streamlining is urgently needed-not more piecemeal solutions to mounting problems.
Mr. Speaker, there are three basic areas of decentralization I wish to touch on, first, the constitutional division of powers. Decentralization is a theme running through the report on the Constitution of Canada produced by the special joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons in June, 1972. I see in the chamber this afternoon the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. Mac-Guigan) who was co-chairman of that committee. I would welcome his contribution to the debate. After recommending a new constitution, the committee's second recommendation was as follows:
A new Canadian constitution should be based on functional considerations, which would lead to greater decentralization of government powers in areas touching cultural and social policy and to greater centralization of powers which have important economic effects at the national level. Functional considerations also require greater decentralization in many areas of government administration.
The principal way in which constitutional decentralization can be brought about is contained in recommendation No. 50 which sets the division of powers in a more modern context as follows:
Concurrent powers which predominantly affect the national interest should grant paramountcy to federal parliament and those which predominantly affect provincial or local interests should grant paramountcy to the provincial legislature.
Therefore, a complete policy on decentralization begins with full support of the constitutional committee's recommendations on decentralization and a commitment to implement them. A more functional allocation of governmental powers will benefit all regions.
As the President of the Treasury Board has himself noted: "Alienation exists in other parts of Canada, especially in the west. The reason for this is that the federal government appears insensitive and unresponsive, just as it used to seem to Quebeckers." In every area of Canada people feel that the constitution is preventing their governments from doing what they would like to see them do.
The committee proposes an expansion of provincial powers in such areas as income support, criminal law, marriage and divorce, educational TV, taxing powers and international arrangements. The committee supports limitation of federal powers with respect to appointments to the Senate and the Supreme Court and with respect to federal spending in fields of provincial jurisdiction. Corre-
Constitution of Canada
spondingly, greater centralization is necessary in the regulation of the economy. Hence, there should be a transfer of some existing provincial powers to the federal parliament, for example, an increase in federal jurisdiction over air and water pollution, international and interprovincial trade and commerce, incomes, securities regulation, financial institutions, unfair competition and foreign ownership.
The constitutional committee made a major recommendation concerning decentralization in the field of social security: the federal government would determine over-all spending in such programs as old age pensions, supplements and family allowances, and the provinces would determine how this total was to be distributed within limits to preserve national standards and maintain the principle of redistributing income.
There is today a great deal of confusion over jurisdiction and increasing political rivalry in promoting bigger social benefits. Integrated economic-social planning between the federal and provincial governments is imperative to prevent the escalation of universal benefits into a welfare state. Strategies for growth, housing and transportation are but three of the items in which the people will best be served by the three levels of government working closely together.
In considering ways to decentralization it should be reaffirmed that the federal parliament must retain the primary responsibility for general economic policy in the country. Thus, decentralization does not rule out centralization in primary areas. The federal parliament must have sufficient economic powers to regulate and influence the economy. However, in fulfilling this constitutional responsibility of centralization, the federal government should explore more ways of decentralizing its operation so that federal policies can be regionally adapted.
It is not satisfactory to leave this matter to the new committee of officials dealing with federal-provincial relations under the terms of Bill C-38-for the authority and role of the House of Commons should not be diminished. As the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) has said, "There is an inexorable danger that these new processes we are developing will bypass parliament and will mean that decisions are taken at some other place; and it is this place where, under our system, decisions are supposed to be taken."
I come now, Mr. Speaker, to the second item under the general heading of decentralization; that is to say, decentralizing federal government departments. Here the news is not quite so good. The importance of our policy reference to the constitution should not be diminished, for complete reform of present incompatibilities takes us directly to the constitution. However, a new constitution cannot be achieved overnight. On the other hand, we do not need a new constitution in order to improve administration, but only a new outlook. The injection of the judgments and feelings of Canadians across the country into a more regionalized government service would be tangible proof that the central government wishes to reach out to all Canadians.
12240

March 29, 1976
Constitution of Canada
Historically, 25 per cent of federal civil servants work in the Ottawa-Hull area, with three-quarters dispersed throughout the rest of Canada. The United States appears to do a better job of decentralizing, since only 12 per cent of the American public service is in and around Washington, D.C.
More importantly, in Canada the decision-making process is still clearly centred in Ottawa; only 14 per cent of senior executives are located outside the national capital region. Most executives have had no field experience and they do not want to go to regional centres because they believe their prospects for career advancement reside primarily in the national capital region. How can the federal government be made more sensitive to the needs and aspirations of Canadians when ambitious public servants consider field assignments to be equivalent to exile?
How, indeed, can we believe that the federal government is serious about decentralization when we see in the 197677 estimates that the federal public works department will spend more money on new capital construction in the city of Ottawa alone, $65 million, than in the entire four western provinces and the northern territories combined, $43 million? In fact, there will be more federal capital spending in Hull, $70 million, than in the entire west and north.
As an Albertan, I note that of the 74 capital construction projects to be carried out next year, only two new ones are found within Alberta-government buildings in Calgary and Lethbridge, with nothing, incidentally, in Edmonton. In addition to the Ottawa-Hull national capital region, Quebec will get 16 high-priced projects worth almost $93 million. Surely, I tell myself, there can be no connection between voting patterns and the awarding of public works projects in a government of such high principle that serves all the people!
That is why the present federal government's announced policies on decentralization give an illusion of improvement without ensuring the reality. Only a start has been made. Recent steps by the federal government have been the relocation of the Royal Canadian Mint in Winnipeg; announced intention of having 70 per cent of the staff of DREE in regional offices and 30 per cent in Ottawa, reversing the present proportion-only 270 Ottawa civil servants affected; the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce extending business counselling assistance to three new areas and delegating, on an experimental basis, to regional offices some granting authority. Since the government has determined that we must have Petro-Canada- our party voted against it-at least it is in Calgary and not Ottawa.
The government points with pride to the move of the supply department's cheque redemption control division to the Gaspe town of Matane, providing 250 jobs and a $2.3 million payroll. What happens to the civil servants who do not want to move? Why, they are given the option of finding jobs elsewhere in the civil service. No wonder we have a hard time distinguishing between decentralization and duplication. As the Montreal Star has noted, as long as decentralization is seen as merely a synonym for pork-barrelling, public confidence in a necessary and overdue program is likely to be weak.
The last annual report of the national capital commission suggests that "it may be possible" to reduce the

percentage of the federal public service in the capital from 25 per cent to 20 per cent. This 5 per cent shift could involve 25,000 jobs. But the Ottawa civil servants aren't worried. The report says it will take 25 years to attain its objectives. Yet the Treasury Board President has said that decentralizing it to get "the highest priority". What does the government's decentralization committee have to say about this contradiction? And, by the way, of whom is this committee composed, when do they meet, and when will they report?
Decentralizing the decision-making process is of far more value than redistributing a handful of civil servants. The joint committee on the constitution of Canada recognized this and stated:
Most Crown corporations could have their headquarters outside Ottawa, as many already have. Federal departments like agriculture, energy, mines and resources, environment, national defence and transport could have their principal offices elsewhere, and many other departments could give their regional offices more authority. Even when Ottawa must remain the effective centre of administration, a greater effort can be made to encourage regional input.
The western premiers, at the Western Economic Opportunities Conference, called for the establishment of industrial "centres of excellence" throughout the various regions of Canada. These centres would be based on natural and human resources, supported by research and marketing assistance to develop a vital economic unit capable of serving national and international markets. Such a program concept suggests clear initiative on the part of the federal government in the establishment and support of new centres of industrial activity in Canada. It would involve decentralization of the technical expertise of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce to plan and support the development of such centres, and the major funding of research activities and new industrial enterprise in cooperation with other departments of the federal government.
We can see, now, the necessity of the federal government permitting the provincial governments and various local organizations to participate in the planning of broad economic development policies, in establishing regional industrial priorities, and in the development and implementation of programs. There should be, in short, decentralization of decision-making power on assistance programs, and strengthening of regional offices.
I come now, Mr. Speaker, to the third and last item, intergovernmental relations. We have seen that constitutional reform is a long-range goal. Decentralization of the administration, while attainable in the near future, still requires structural changes. What can be accomplished immediately is more inter-governmental co-operation. A fresh spirit of federal government co-operation and consultation will do wonders in achieving decentralization of the decision-making process.
The municipalities, especially, will be helped via this method, since there is little hope for the entrenchment of expanded municipal rights in a revised constitution. Facing the crushing super problem of urbanization, the municipalities must negotiate a better tax position with the provincial and federal governments. Recognizing the plight, indeed the trap, of municipalities, the federal government could find a structural way for the inclusion of local government in the federal and provincial decision-
March 29, 1976

making process. In this way, local officials would be sharing more directly in the management of urbanization-a complex social problem-rather than merely finding ways to cope with the effects of urbanization.
The joint municipal committee on intergovernmental relations which reported a couple of years ago told us, in short, that the role of local government today no longer satisfies the needs of society experiencing the process of urbanization. In brief, the federal and provincial governments cannot solve the problems of an urbanized society without the link to the community provided by local government. The municipal governments must have expanded methods of increasing their tax revenue. That is the nub of the problem, Mr. Speaker. Therefore, the municipalities want a restructuring of revenue-generating capacity and involvement in the federal and provincial decision-making process. Their demand for more participation is supported by the joint committee on the constitution. Their recommendation No. 67 says:
In the light of the injustice done municipalities by their having to rely on the property tax for the bulk of their revenue, there should be a sharing of tax fields between governments that would allow municipalities direct access to other sources of revenue.
A three-level task force of representatives from Ottawa, the provinces and the municipalities have been studying for nearly two years the problems of public finance. The report, which will soon be completed, was commissioned by the last national tri-level conference in Edmonton in 1973. It is easily predictable that the report will insist that the cities are running out of money to build and service the structures needed for an additional urban population of 12 million in the next 20 years. The property tax is a hopelessly outmoded method of revenue-raising, incapable of providing the gigantic amounts of public capital needed to continue building our cities.
I see my time has practically elapsed, Mr. Speaker, if it has not already, and I would ask the permission of the House to continue for a few minutes so I can conclude my remarks.

speechtext: Agreed.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED FEDERAL GOVERNMENT CONSIDERATION OF COMPREHENSIVE PLAN OF DECENTRALIZED GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, and my colleagues. True, decentralization calls for massive changes in the financial system of Canada so that municipalities can provide the public transportation, housing, water and social services demanded by urbanization. Grants by senior governments that want the political credit for handing out money are not the answer; today there are so many millions of dollars of transfer payments being issued from one government office to another that it is impossible to keep track of it all, let alone provide accountability to the people.
Despite the constitutional inadequacies, the federal government has basic urban responsibilities that can only be exercised by partnership, not paternalism. A national urban strategy is desperately needed. But, as Toronto metro chairman Paul Godfrey, who is also president of the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities said:
Constitution of Canada
"I fear the national urban strategy will be a long time coming, and that when it comes it will be revealed as having been developed by a group of civil servants peering blankly at the rest of the country through the smoke of their campfires on the Ottawa River."
Nowhere is a fair-minded federal policy more urgently needed than in the funding of rapid transit, which is the backbone of urban growth. In the 1974 election campaign, the federal government promised a significant contribution toward urban transportation capital investment. This was good news to Edmonton in the process of constructing Canada's third subway system. But the government reneged on this promise by imposing a specious definition of "commuter system" that excluded rapid transit systems that operate within municipalities. So much for any financial aid to Edmonton. This promise was fulfilled in the same manner that the promise of federal assistance-made by the Treasury Board President-for the Edmonton Cultural and Convention Center was fulfilled. That is to say, nothing. Is it any wonder that out west we no longer trust this overly-centralized federal government that is making such a mockery of the aspiration to better intergovernmental relations?
As far as we in Edmonton are concerned, the federal government's policy in urban transportation is deficient in funding, scope, timing and concept and has discriminated particularly against Edmonton. Now, when we learn of proposals to terminate the CNR transcontinental passenger service through Edmonton, we are understandably upset as well as fighting mad at a federal government that refuses to recognize the importance of Canada's fifth largest city as a key distribution and terminal centre in western Canada. The industrial growth of northern Alberta is dynamic; 90 per cent of all projects proposed or under construction are north of Red Deer. All modes of transportation, including rail passenger transport should be developed and improved, rather than eliminated.
Mr. Speaker, my conclusion has admittedly been lengthy. But true decentralization is both vast and deep. Last week, the Edmonton area members of parliament met with the city administration in Edmonton and the chamber of commerce. It is clear to me that the leaders of our community want to see implemented a new philosophy of government that will meet modern social pressures. For the quality of life at the community level will continue to be impeded unless the anomalies and pressures faced by the cities are alleviated.
Above all, decentralization demands a willingness by the federal government to implement a new system of revenue-sharing to help community leaders all over Canada cope with urbanization.

speechtext: The more government, the better, is yours.

speechtext: Generally speaking, I find I am in agreement with him more extensively than I am in disagreement. I want to state at the beginning, for the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), that liberal philosophy is, more government where necessary and where it is beneficial to the people.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED FEDERAL GOVERNMENT CONSIDERATION OF COMPREHENSIVE PLAN OF DECENTRALIZED GOVERNMENT
speechtext: No, the more government, the better the government; that is your philosophy.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED FEDERAL GOVERNMENT CONSIDERATION OF COMPREHENSIVE PLAN OF DECENTRALIZED GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
No, that is NDP philosophy. I am not going to speak about their philosophy today. I may have something to say about it sometime, but not in this context.
I should like to make clear one concern I have at the very beginning, and that is the enormous emphasis the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona placed on municipalities. I find this very curious, because surely decentralization is a lot more than, and not only, that. Also, the municipalities and their problems involve a lot more than this matter of decentralization. Perhaps I might make this a little bit more specific. In the province of Ontario the problem, in many respects, has been the fact that the provincial government in recent years has created, as a kind of emanation from Queen's Park, where the provincial government is located, a further centralization. The system of regional governments has been very badly worked out, as a result of which the costs of government have actually increased, yet the services to the people have not. There have been two competing bureaucracies set up in the same localities.
I do not think one can simply consider the problems of cities in the context of decentralization. There are a lot of things involved. I agree with the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona that the property tax is not a suitable tax, but this surely is not a matter of decentralization but, rather, a question involving the form of taxation you are going to use. I think we all would like to see some changes made.
The end result of the suggestion that this is to be all laid at the door of the federal government will be a perpetuation of the idea that no provincial government, like that of Ontario, has any authority or responsibility in the area, particularly if people think it is the federal government that should change the plight of our cities in Ontario when in fact it is the provincial government that has the primary responsibility. I do not think we do a service to the cause of decentralization or of reform if we do not recognize that it is the provincial governments in Canada which ought to clean up this bloody mess. I will come back to that issue in a few moments, Mr. Speaker.
I want, first, to refer to the Special Joint Committee On the Constitution of Canada which presented its report just a little over four years ago. That committee recommended both more centralization and more decentralization; more centralization, generally speaking, in respect of economic powers, and more decentralization in respect of social powers and the administration of federal government powers, and more decentralization in the federal powers which are retained in the interim before any changes can be made.

I want to quote briefly from that report. The hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona has given a pretty good summary of the committee's report, but I should like to bring it together in two or three sentences. I quote from the committee report at page 2:
We have spoken of the need for an increase in both centralization and decentralization, depending on functional considerations. In our view greater decentralization in areas of culture and social policy would benefit all the provinces. We propose such decentralization for reasons of functionalism and flexibility, and to meet the regional differences which became obvious to us in the course of our hearings.
The committee went on the specify some of the areas in which decentralization should occur. The hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona has already referred to these. Again quoting from the report:
On the other hand, greater centralization is necessary in the regulation of the economy. Hence there should be a transfer of some existing provincial powers to the federal parliament.
Again there are some examples to which the hon. member has already referred. Then my final quotation from that report:
At the same time, we favour considerable administrative decentralization in the operations of the federal government. This change of administrative direction requires no change in the constitution. It does require a change of heart. It involves the recognition that geographically Canada is a very, very large country.
Although parliament recognizes that the considerations of that committee were constitutional ones, and no constitutional changes have taken place which reflect its recommendations, it is nevertheless fair to say that there have been many changes in federal policy as a result of the recommendations of that committee. The process of regular intergovernmental consultation has been set up, and especially the tripartite consultation between the federal government, the provinces, and the municipalities-not without considerable difficulties, I might add, in the case of this latter form of consultation because of continuing provincial objections to any formal meeting in which the federal government actually meets face to face with the municipalities. Of course we have disregarded that kind of objection which the provinces continue to make.
In other areas as well, even in the matter of the appointment of senators from the Yukon and the Northwest Territories, which creates a greater regional balance in the Senate, there was a fulfilment of the recommendations in the committee's report, as well as the very significant movement which occurred in the federal government's family allowance program, which was again the carrying out of the recommendations which the committee made with respect to income support measures.
I would like to quote again from the committee's report, recommendation 84, paragraph (3), which reads:
Demographic grants (old age pensions, family allowances and youth allowances) and guaranteed income payments (guaranteed income supplements) should be matters of concurrent jurisdiction with limited provincial paramountcy as to the scale of benefits and the allocation of federal funds among these income support programs.
This kind of limited provincial paramountcy was written into the Family Allowance Act as a simple federal statute. It could be changed subsequently, but for all practical purposes the result is the same as if it were a constitution-
March 29, 1976

al change because no government is likely to change it without giving it careful consideration.
I could go on to talk about the multicultural program and other ways in which the government has implemented the report at a non-constitutional level, but I merely want to sketch the fact that there has been a considerable change in government policy as a result of the recommendations of the committee.
Not the least important of those changes has been that with respect to the general decentralization of administration which has been occurring. Partly this is just a question of giving better service to people in various areas to make sure that they are adequately served by federal offices in their areas, but I think it is more important than that; it is a chance for open decision making and shared decision-making. The hon. member for Edmonton-Strath-cona has referred to this and I agree thoroughly with what he had to say on it. I think this is the primary advantage of decentralization, and decentralization at the decision-making level is the most important kind. I suppose that sharing economic benefits from decentralized government offices across the country is another advantage which may occur, but I do not think that this pork-barrel aspect, if I may refer to it that way, is anything like the main reason for decentralization.
I think we should also recognize that modern technology itself does not necessarily require centralization. We should take the unemployment insurance program as an example of this. When the Unemployment Insurance Act was changed, and also computers were used for the first time in putting the whole system on a recorded basis in one central place, it was thought that the new system would be that there would be one office-in Ontario it is Belleville-and that all the operations of the Unemployment Insurance Commission which affect clients would be in Belleville. That is where the computer was to be, and from where everything was to work.
After two or three years' experience it came to be realized that this type of centralization was one which gave very poor service to the clients, and indeed was one which did not adequately take into account the kind of varied decisions which have to be made with respect to particular clients' cases. About two years ago the present minister instituted a new program of decentralization in which the regional offices which had been disbanded were upgraded, the local offices were re-established, and new local offices were established.
In addition to that there is a program for the establishment of computer terminals at most of the offices across the country, so that when the program is completed across the country the client in a particular office who goes to the wicket will be able to get very complete information as to the status of his claim right there through the use of computer terminals, and he will be able to get a decision right there from the insurance officer, which is reflected at once in the computer, and on the basis of which payment is made immediately. In other words, he gets first-quality service and he gets it face-to-face from the people who make the decisions, but because of the computer he gets it much more quickly. He would not get this if the system were centralized in Belleville and not plugged into the
Constitution of Canada
local community through the local unemployment insurance office.
That is an indication of the way in which government programs can reflect a desire for decentralization, and one in which the benefits are not only for the individual but also for the system because the system functions better, and even a systems specialist would see that, if he is not one whose basis is entirely mathematical.
I think that there is considerable agreement between the positions that the hon. member has advanced and those I am here enunciating, but again I should like to repeat my concern over the fact that for him this seems to come down to the municipal question. I think that the person whom decentralization should serve is the citizen. It is primarily for the purpose of giving him input into decision-making, and the proper service, as well as a regional share in his government's services. I think that any benefits that may occur to municipalities as a result of this are really incidental, and I do not think that they are primarily the responsibility of the federal government, certainly not under this kind of program.
We have to put the responsibility for municipal problems where it properly belongs, and if we do not do that, as I mentioned before, we are going to perpetuate a false impression of our provincial governments, which are not doing their jobs, because we are creating the impression that it is the federal government, which should be solving these problems.
Municipal problems today are indeed staggering. I am most familiar with those in Ontario where I see, as a result of the half worked-out and badly worked-out system of regional government, that the system has been made worse. We have a government in Ontario which is handing over to the municipalities the costs which the provincial government should be absorbing. The provincial government is saving money by making municipalities pay more, seemingly without any regard for the position in which the municipalities find themselves, and all this is being done without any relief from a proper tax base. That is a very serious problem in the province of Ontario, but it is an Ontario problem, one which the people of Ontario should solve. I dare say they should solve it by changing the government, but that is not a problem which we can solve in this House.

If I may say to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), we may at least have some common ground in our attitude toward the government of Ontario.
I just want to say that I think we must be careful not to make this kind of mistake, not to think of these problems which are provincial as being federal.
The hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona is quite right in saying that there has to be a federal urban presence. The federal government itself is present under probably some 30 programs in cities, and it has a great duty to co-operate with the provinces and with the municipalities

March 29, 1976
Constitution of Canada
in planning, especially in the area of urban transportation. It should be co-operating more than it is, and I agree with the hon. member on that point as well, but the fact is that this responsibility of the federal government toward the municipalities is still primarily a peripheral responsibility. It is not peripheral in respect of transportation, but the heart of the municipal problem is a provincial problem, and it is only the provinces which can solve that problem. We have to keep the focus where it belongs.
I think it has been useful for us to have had a chance to look at the problem of decentralization. The general recognition of the need for decentralization is one of the most striking phenomena of today. This is true of business as well as of government. I do not think we should consider this as anything which is peculiar to governments alone. It is something which is a general part of human life today. As the hon. member himself suggested, it is nevertheless compatible with greater government at the international level, but only to the extent that it carefully preserves the independence and the right to make decisions which various countries around the globe have. I certainly join the hon. member in saying-and I think he did say this-that decentralization does not necessarily mean less government in the world; it means more careful government, government which is more carefully tailored to the needs of the people.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED FEDERAL GOVERNMENT CONSIDERATION OF COMPREHENSIVE PLAN OF DECENTRALIZED GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext: I should like to pose a question to the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. MacGuigan). He said that I put a great deal of emphasis on having municipalities accept their own responsibility for property which they have on their doorsteps. I did dwell on that. I should like to ask the hon. member if he agrees that, without a new revenue sharing formula in this country, the municipalities are handicapped and cannot solve the problem of urbanization; that that is precisely the reason a national urban policy is needed with an initiative by the federal government which will help the municipalities to find a way which will be proper under the constitution for revenue sharing; and that it is not, consequently, correct to say that it is only the problem of the municipalities when in fact the power to tax at the principal levels in this country is held and maintained by the federal government.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED FEDERAL GOVERNMENT CONSIDERATION OF COMPREHENSIVE PLAN OF DECENTRALIZED GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if I may briefly reply, I agree with the hon. member that the problem is with respect to revenue sharing, but it is revenue sharing by the provinces. I do not think that it requires any changes between the provinces and the federal government. It requires a willingness on the part of the provinces to share their revenues with municipalities. It requires the provinces to share their income tax resources with the municipalities, but as I kept repeating it is the provinces which have the responsibility.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED FEDERAL GOVERNMENT CONSIDERATION OF COMPREHENSIVE PLAN OF DECENTRALIZED GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased that the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Roche) raised the question he brought before the House through notice of motion No. 37, which I do not need to

read now. It is a motion which deals first with the constitutional relations between the provinces and the federal government i.e. the constitutional separation of powers, or the division of powers secondly, with the decentralization of the decision-making process among the federal departments and, lastly, with the improvement of intergovernmental relations.
Of course, this is an opportunity to speak in detail of any subject pertaining to the constitutional problem. Before raising the question of the division of powers as such and that of the powers which should remain within the provinces or those which the federal government should retain, I would simply like to add a few words about the question of the patriation of the Canadian constitution which the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) raised a few weeks ago.
I just want to say that I am happy to see that our Prime Minister has decided once again to contact the provincial premiers and ask their consent in order to repatriate the Canadian Constitution. For that is what the Prime Minister has done. He has contacted again the provincial first ministers and asked them to agree to the repatriation of the Constitution. However, the Prime Minister said that this time there should not be any obstacle in the way of the agreement, as was the case for Quebec and Victoria, in 1971. After numerous concessions by several provinces which granted certain demands from Quebec, this province refused once again to agree to the Victoria Charter and to the patriation of the Constitution.
Quebec has been acting in this manner for many years. I do not have the document in hand, but it is a fact that Quebec has always refused to give its agreement because it demanded certain a number of constitutional concessions from the federal government in the areas of immigration, of communications, and of social security, at least before 1971. Since then, there have been some administrative arrangements and apparently the question is more or less settled. But Quebec has always refused its consent to the federal government and the other provinces for the repatriation of the Constitution unless the other provinces and the federal government made concessions in those areas.
I believe that Quebec, an important province of this country, has the right to demand certain things, perhaps because of its peculiar cultural characteristics. I believe that the interests of the entire country are equally important here. I was deeply disappointed, especially in 1971, because for the first time we seemed to have reached an agreement about the repatriation of the Constitution as well as on a amendment formula, and furthermore, the Victoria Charter provided some safeguards for the French language in the country.
And for a French-speaking Canadian living outside Quebec, this is important. However, it is the province of Quebec who rejected that safeguard.
In my opinion,-

beneficial to them. However, an Acadian who represents the first Frenchmen who came to North America and Canada will never accept that his language depends on Quebecers. subsubtopic: SUGGESTED FEDERAL GOVERNMENT CONSIDERATION OF COMPREHENSIVE PLAN OF DECENTRALIZED GOVERNMENT

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED FEDERAL GOVERNMENT CONSIDERATION OF COMPREHENSIVE PLAN OF DECENTRALIZED GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Many years before! I shall look up the history books for the benefit of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of External Affairs, and I shall report to her. I merely say that Champlain came to Nova Scotia before going to Quebec.
I would like to say that by systematically objecting to the repatriation of the constitution, Quebec takes a position that smacks of blackmail. It is saying to the rest of Canada, perhaps to Anglophones or to the Ontario people who want to repatriate the constitution, that between them, Ottawa and the provinces, they are trying to find a way to amend the constitution that would be suitable to all concerned. And, in my opinion, to insist on obtaining some constitutional concessions even before accepting the patriation itself without amendment is almost blackmail.
And I can say that I am proud that our Prime Minister has indicated he would again contact the provinces and ask their consent, and that this time he would urge Parliament to act unilaterally to bring home the Canadian constitution since is has never been here before, and then we would try with the provinces to find some means of amendment which would protect Quebec as well as Ontario or British Columbia, which also had certain reservations in 1971 about an amendment formula.
Once the constitution is back home, and this is my opinion not necessarily the government's, if Quebec still wants to frustrate an agreement on an amendment formula, both Houses will have the responsibility to see to it. There must be an amendment formula attached to the Canadian constitution once it has been brought back. That is not to say that the federal Parliament should unilaterally amend the constitution, but it should, for example under the 1971 formula, give Quebec and Ontario a right of veto, and I think it should even give one, under certain circumstances, to British Columbia. I am no expert in constitutional law, but I think that such a mode of amendment could not be considered as unreasonable.
In my opinion the federal Parliament, the government, should, when the constitution is repatriated, consult with the provinces regarding an amendment formula and try to win their consent, but even then, the federal Parliament ought to assume its responsibilities and try to obtain an amendment consensus. I emphasize that we should not amend the constitution unilaterally; this would not be acceptable even though it would be constitutionally sound but it would be most unwise politically. We have the responsibility to deal with issues such as the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Roche) is bringing up here. Unless the constitution is repatriated and a consensus is reached regarding the amendment, we in Parliament, and Canadians in general, will not be able to amend the constitution. I am aware that other hon. members wish to speak. To conclude I shall say that I have been extremely sur-
Constitution of Canada
prised to note the position taken by the premier of my province when he recently announced that he would side with Premier Bourassa, in a very intricate official statement. It was rather difficult to understand clearly what his intentions were but we inferred that he was going to enter into an agreement with Mr. Bourassa in order to take a stand agains the Prime Minister because, apparently, he was concerned that the Prime Minister would do that within the context of partisan politics.
Naturally, that is not true; I feel his own remarks smell far more of party politics than anything else because there is not much logic in his release unless it is political logic. And I feel that the expression "political logic" is a bit contradictory in itself because, as we know, in politics there is often very little logic or reason. I merely want to say that Mr. Hatfield wants to join a strange partner because where the linguistic question was concerned, Bill 22, they certainly were not allies. In fact, Mr. Hatfield came quite close to intervening at the Supreme Court of Canada. At least; he sent observers.
We wondered what we had to say to Quebec concerning the linguistic question, within the province, in its own sphere. But I find it strange that Mr. Hatfield should have decided on that strange alliance. Perhaps patriation of the constitution and some amendments to it, might give linguistic rights to the Francophones outside Quebec, on the one hand, and on the other, reaffirm the linguistic rights of the Anglophones in Quebec, and give Canada the possibility of amending its constitution: that might, in turn, give certain advantages to New Brunswick as well as other provinces.
I must say then that I am happy the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona brought up the matter of the constitution, because it gave us the opportunity of discussing it.

The patriation discussion that has been going on in the last little while is an example of confrontation which
