AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 8 p.m.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Lalonde that Bill S-31, to amend the Quarantine Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND APPLICATION TO DANGEROUS DISEASES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when debate on the second reading of Bill S-31 was interrupted at five o'clock I had indicated our readiness to support it. As I said, in line with what had been said by the minister and the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk), we live in an age in which new diseases and viruses turn up unexpectedly. In this age of fast, mass transportation the Government of Canada must be able to cope with persons or vehicles which might bring new or strange diseases to this country. The bill deals not only with persons; it deals also with vehicles of all kinds, whether they travel on land, by sea, or in the air.

As I said, we asked ourselves some questions about the bill when we first saw it. First, we wanted to be sure that it does not interfere with basic civil rights, or does not do things which might be done under the Immigration Act and thus deny certain rights which would otherwise apply. We cannot find that there is any unwarranted interference with civil liberties. The bill does not deny a Canadian the right to come back to this country, or a visitor's or an immigrant's right, under the Immigration Act, to come here. It provides for a person suspected of having a certain dangerous disease to be put in quarantine for the time it takes that disease to incubate. I need not spell it out. As I say, we looked at the bill with the question of civil rights in our minds and find nothing objectionable in it on that score.
As I say, the bill requires certain persons to be quarantined for the length of time it takes a strange or dangerous disease to incubate. After all, even the astronauts, heroes though they were, who came back to the United States from the moon were put in quarantine lest they had picked up some strange disease in that part of the universe.
The other question we asked ourselves was if the bill provides for powers too wide for parliament to give to the executive. I notice that the hon. member for Athabasca expressed concern on this point. We can deal with it when the bill is in committee. It seems to me that the bill contains protections. Quarantine officers are given certain rights and powers. If a quarantine officers feels he must do more than is permitted by the legislation he must get an order from the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde). If the aggrieved person feels that the order is unfair, there is provision in the bill for an appearance before a judge within a matter of hours. It strikes me, therefore, that there is a reasonable balance between the situation which can develop if someone is found to be the carrier of a new virus or strange disease and the rule of law. In other words, we do not want to give the executive unlimited power. I do not find this bill offensive on that score.
I echo the concern raised by the hon. member for Athabasca when he mentioned that about 40 million persons cross our borders every year and wondered if we can solve the problem of disease control simply by passing a bill. I also echo his concern about our limited facilities for checking strange diseases and for putting people in quarantine. But the bill seems to make the kinds of amendments to the Quarantine Act which are called for in these times; therefore, Sir, we are prepared to give the bill second reading so that it can go to committee where witnesses can appear and where we can ask any further questions which ought to be answered.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND APPLICATION TO DANGEROUS DISEASES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my comments on Bill S-31, an act to amend the Quarantine Act, will be brief. Some questions I had anticipated asking were answered by the minister this afternoon, or raised by the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk) and by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles).
I acknowledge receipt of three documents from the department which I found extremely useful. I shall allude to them in discussing this bill. Some aspects of the documentation are paradoxical, in that they raise certain questions. Although I have no intention of going through these
March 29, 1976

documents in detail, I want to make one or two references to what in each document I think is somewhat of a paradoxical situation.
One document is rather intriguing. It is entitled "International Health Determination of Lassa Fever Problem". It is particularly pertinent. It was written, I gather, by Dr. Sprenger of the department, a senior consultant, Quarantine and Regulatory Medical Services Branch, Department of Health and Welfare. It is an excellent document outlining Lassa fever.
As I understand it, this particular document on Lassa fever and Marburg disease is really the proto-type of the type of problem that brought about the implementation of the particular piece of legislation we see at this time. As I indicated, there are some aspects of this document about which I am concerned. I want to quote one section. It reads:
In contingency planning against Lassa fever, the new international dimension we are facing is not so much control of one of the scourges of the past as it is taking steps to prevent the emergence of a new plague in Canada and in countries of the world with which we have direct transportation air links.
Vivid illustration of the inadequacy of relying on any voluntary system of control to curtail international transportation of patients was the self-arranged return earlier this year to London by commercial airline from West Africa of a doctor stricken with Lassa fever. The public has a right to expect compliance powers to exist for the effective enforcement of quarantine control. Urgent action is vital when faced with such an inadvertent importation, in order to minimize the risks. The risks when dealing with diseases caused by the dangerous pathogens can be considerable.
With the legislation before us it seems that we are embarking upon a whole new era of quarantine. There is no question that there are great powers given to the minister and, indeed, to the quarantine officer. At some appropriate time I hope the minister will respond to this whole new line of progress in terms of quarantine, particularly when in the past we have had essentially a voluntary system other than those entities to which the minister referred. This is important. We must recognize that we are embarking on a new area in terms of quarantine and new disease entities.
I received a document earlier today entitled "Canadian Quarantine Manual". This is particularly pertinent. I wish to quote from Section 4.2.1. which reads as follows:
The Federal Quarantine Act was promulgated the 1st of January 1972-
The minister made reference to that earlier this afternoon.
-and is an Act to reduce the hazard of introduction into Canada of infectious or contagious diseases. It will be noted that the format of the Regulations has been changed from the previous specific type of format applicable to Maritime trade to a discretionary type of format more applicable to the speed of current international air travel.
What concerns me somewhat is that the minister indicated that we had dramatic changes to the Quarantine Act in 1972 which was promulgated January 1 of that year. We now have new amendments to the act with the prototype Lassa fever and Marburg disease being given as the reasons for them. I find this strange. As the minister indicated, Lassa fever was a well recognized entity in 1969. It was recognized as being a very virulent type of organism with
Quarantine Act
a high morbidity rate. The same can be said of Marburg disease. If one refers to the document I mentioned earlier entitled "International Health Dimensions of the Lassa Fever Problem", it is well illustrated that both these disease entities were well known to medical circles and in the international community as being a deadly serious virus.
The minister has some explaining to do as to why we are seeing these amendments at this time. If in fact that concern existed in 1972 when it was promulgated, I cannot help but think we should have seen the amendments at that time.
The last document concerns the Canadian contingency plan with respect to Lassa fever. The hon. member for Athabasca referred to this earlier. For those who are interested, it gives an excellent introduction on the disease itself and situations in which the virus organism can present itself. In addition, it deals with the principles underlying the federal government's participation in the program.
This implies two things to me. It seems to be somewhat in contradistinction to what the minister stated later today. I assume the minister implied that at this time there are only four disease entities-cholera, plague, smallpox, and yellow fever-that are part of the Quarantine Act and in fact no other disease has been listed. However, as I read this particular contingency plan it is implied that Lassa fever may in fact be on this list. This is a specific question which could be asked at a later date.
As was indicated earlier, it is not certain from the documentation whether in fact we have a capability to carry out the particular principles enunciated in this document. At any rate I want to recognize and acknowledge the importance of these documents. I plan to study them in more depth. I have additional questions related to these documents that I would like to ask at a later time.
We are a global community that has become much smaller with the passage of time, particularly with the jet age. Because of that we are far more vulnerable to contagious and infectious disease. I agree in principle with the minister that we need the capability to prevent certain infectious or contagious diseases that may prove to be very detrimental to the health of Canadians. They may be highly communicable and have a high degree of morbidity.
As I interpret the legislation, there is a necessity to be able to provide the facilities and also to have a contingency type of plan to look after Canadians returning to Canada, who may well have a contagious disease, for treatment and diagnostic purposes.
There are several questions that, in my view, have not been answered. One particular area is with regard to federal-provincial jurisdiction. It is well recognized that the federal government has a responsibility in terms of the Quarantine Act. This was alluded to earlier today. It is also an accepted fact that the traditional health care system is a provincial responsibility.
I wish to pose a hypothetical question because I am not clear as to the jurisdiction in this area. In the great number of cases one would see, in terms of contagious or communicable disease, that type of individual who has been visiting, in this instance, let us say West Africa, and who has returned home to his particular province. Four or five days

March 29, 1976
Quarantine Act
later he develops symptoms that are consistent with the particular disease entity, in this instance Lassa fever. I am not clear in my own mind where jurisdiction now falls, whether this is a matter strictly under the jurisdiction of the province itself or whether the federal government has a direct responsibility and can intervene if it feels it has information at its disposal which would suggest there may well be a health hazard to Canada.
As the minister outlined earlier in his comments this afternoon, the four diseases listed in the Quarantine Act at present are cholera, plague, smallpox, and yellow fever. I am not certain as to the means the minister and his department would use to determine what other pathogens would be listed under the Quarantine Act. I am not even sure how they would be determined. Do we really have the epidemiological capability to make this type of determination? We need far more information about the staff within the department and the follow-up capability which exists. It is important to know what consultation has gone on between the provinces and the federal government and, of course, it is extremely important to know what has happened in the international context. Has there been input from the World Health Organization?
The minister did indicate, if I understood him correctly, that if a particular pathogen is thought to be dangerous enough it would be listed by order in council. And if I understood him correctly, that listing could be terminated at any time by order in council. Is that correct?
I am also interested, and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has alluded to this, in the possible infringement of civil liberties involved. This is another important area which should be looked at carefully during the committee stage. I alluded to that earlier in my comments.
There is one other aspect on which I should like to spend a moment or two because I had hoped, when this quarantine bill was introduced, that the minister was implying a greater concern on the part of the government with respect to tackling the various contagious and infectious diseases which presently exist in Canada.
I know the minister has received various representations in the past regarding the positive role the federal government could and should be playing in combatting these diseases. To give one example, I should like to talk for a moment on the subject of tropical diseases and parasites which are increasing, frankly, at a substantial rate in Canada.
We must recognize that Canada, like many other temperate countries such as England, Sweden or New Zealand, is really faced with these exotic-type diseases because of the global age and because of the jet travel which is now so common. The danger is compounded by the great degree of tourism. Figures were quoted earlier; the figure of 40 million was mentioned in connection with the Canadian tourist industry. And, of course, we are seeing a migration of people from all countries of the world.
The other thing we must recognise is that there have been disturbing reports principally from ports of entry, from major cities including Halifax, Montreal, Edmonton, and Vancouver. Certainly the Toronto General Hospital

with its tropical and parasitic disease clinic could show a very alarming increase in the incidence of tropical and parasitic diseases. I think we must recognise, and I quite agree with the minister in principle, that because of this type of setting and the facility of communication we see today it is highly unlikely that Canada will ever again be free of exotic diseases in the future.
If we look carefully I think we would find it startling that there is no school of tropical medicine within the confines of Canada. I have seen estimates that probably less than one per cent of physicians in Canada have any education or particular experience in the area of tropical or parasitic diseases. It is unfortunate that there seems to be such an indifference at times within the profession and the medical schools. There are so many of these diseases, many of them common to tropical countries etc., and little knowledge is actually imparted through the medical schools and, indeed, by nursing schools. I find this most unfortunate.
We must also recognise that at government levels there has been lack of funding for some of the post-basic education and the training of physicians and nurses, as well as for the training of the technical personnel who are extremely important in this particular specialty of tropical and parasitic diseases.
I hate to come back to the word research because I have talked about it so many times, but it is another area of medical research where the government has really not given the type of support needed to deal with tropical and parasitic diseases. I have also received representations from various people within the profession and within the pharmaceutical industry stating that on occasions we have had difficulty obtaining certain of the drugs, what one might call exotic drugs, necessary to treat some of these tropical diseases which, I want to assure you, Mr. Speaker, do occur and have occurred in Canada. I should also indicate we have many examples of lengthy delays before patients reach the specialized clinics which are at a premium in the Canadian context.
I also want to indicate that we have very little knowledge when we come to discuss the subject of multiple infections, the toxicity of drug reactions, the conditions which can cross the placental barrier, to name just a few of the perplexities associated with the study of tropical and parasitic diseases. I have no intention of lecturing on the issue of tropical and parasitic diseases. I suspect the average individual probably thinks of tropical or parasitic diseases as mainly confined to pinworms. I suspect that anyone who has raised children is well aware of that particular condition.
I want to assure you, Mr. Speaker, there are other threats to health in this area, for example, amoebiasis. If one looks carefully it is endemic in an area such as Toronto. Studies in the province of Saskatchewan have indicated that approximately 30 per cent of the native population in that province have anti-viruses in an endemic form. We must recognise that we escape epidemics in these instances because we do have hygienic facilities and the type of practice in this area which have prevented epidemics up to this point. But we must also recognise that it may lie dormant for life. It is not uncommon at the time of autopsy to find that many patients have suffered from this particu-
March 29, 1976

lar disease. I think this is true of every province across the country.
You might find it of some interest, Mr. Speaker, that malaria was at one time endemic in parts of Canada, in the Kent and Essex counties specifically. I am rather interested in the fact that the anopheles mosquito is still present here-it was reported two or three years ago in Oregon. A soldier returned from Viet Nam-his malaria had not been diagnosed at that point-and visited a picnic area. Mosquitoes in that part were infected, and later a group of nurses who visited the area came down with malaria within a short period of time. This is an indication that some of these diseases which we think of as being extremely rare, which we think could not occur in Canada, do occur.
Many hon. members will recall the Peterborough Petes of the Junior A League who visited Leningrad two years ago. Half the team came down with a severe parasitic infection.
I am simply saying that I hope the minister, in bringing this quarantine bill before us, is thinking beyond the act itself and is paying some recognition to the importance of tropical and parasitic diseases and to some of the other exotic diseases to which he has referred. I am quite concerned that we do not have the capability at this point to handle these diseases despite the importance of the issue and despite the implications of the bill.
May I reiterate that I support the principle of quarantine for certain infectious diseases and in pathogenic cases; but I also suggest that there are many unanswered questions, and that we need greater leadership from the federal government in areas such as tropical and parasitical diseases.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have only a few comments to make in connection with these changes. In general I agree with them. Much has been said before about the need for changes in the present Quarantine Act. The need to cover so-called dangerous diseases is self-evident. Fortunately these diseases are quite rare and hopefully will remain so.
I presume that certain additions may be made to the list by order in council. However, I think it is most important that any additions of so-called dangerous diseases to the list be along the lines of those suggested by the World Health Organization. In other words, I hope we will not act unilaterally in adding so-called dangerous diseases to those already on the list.
Much has also been said about people moving around the world these days, and it is a fact that it is almost impossible within a short period of time properly to screen the average visitor, immigrant or person returning to Canada from abroad.
I should like to make mention some of the changes regarding the handling of suspected cases. At the present time under the Infectious and Contagious Diseases Act the period of detention is not to exceed the prescribed incubation period, and on the authority of the quarantine officer an appeal can be made to the deputy minister of the health service.
Quarantine Act
There are some significant changes in the new subsection (8)(l)(c) under which a person can be detained up to 14 days under the authority of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde). In other words, a quarantine officer must get authority from someone higher up the ladder. On weekends, holidays, and so on I wonder about the chain of command in this regard. Presumably a quarantine officer would have to telephone or communicate in some way with Ottawa.
Knowing what it is like at times to get decisions, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me there may be some trouble in implementing this provision. I would be interested to know what will be the actual mechanism used to enable a quarantine officer or customs officer who suspects someone is suffering from a dangerous disease to take prompt action. I suggest there would be a good many cases that would take three or four days, perhaps even a week, to deal with.
With regard to the provisions dealing with a judicial review the minister must justify to a Supreme Court judge detention in excess of 48 hours unless within that period the suspected case is confirmed. This seems to me to be pushing the time element to the extreme and I have some doubt whether this process could be completed within that period. Any person who is detained can ask the minister to justify before a Supreme Court judge of the province the reason for his detention, which seems to me could lead to delay.
As far as the new section 9 is concerned I have no great problem. I presume that the regulations will be along the line of what is considered reasonable in medical circles and customary throughout the world.
I think some questions can be raised in regard to subsection (7) in that a quarantine officer may act not only when he suspects a person has an infectious and contagious disease, as was the case before, but when he suspects a person has any other disease which may, in the opinion of the quarantine officer, constitute a grave danger to public health in Canada. This immediately raises in my mind the question whether the quarantine officer will be given guidelines, or will he be allowed considerable latitude in deciding what constitutes a grave danger to public health in Canada? A quarantine officer is not a person trained in medicine and presumably will have to rely heavily on guidelines. As the bill is presently written the situation is not too clear. It seems to me possible, as the bill is presently worded, that a quarantine or customs officer acting on his own could in certain instances detain a person unjustifiably.
The amendment to subsection 8(1)(d) is a slight broadening of the original act. In the original act this provision applied to a person who had been in close proximity to someone who was a carrier of a contagious disease or who is in close proximity to someone who is infested with insects. Under this change the person in question need only have been in close proximity to a person who may have, or may be the carrier of an infectious or contagious disease, and this includes people arriving in or departing from Canada. This tends to broaden the area of jurisdiction of the quarantine officer and enables him to work a little more effectively in cases of doubt. He will also carry more responsibility and will have brought into his area of

March 29, 1976
Quarantine Act
jurisdiction considerably more people. This leaves the situation open to abuse and could cause the zealous quarantine officer some unhappiness. I think some guidelines will have to be formulated carefully in this particular area.
Under subsection 8(2) the scope of a quarantine officer's jurisdiction is extended to people arriving in or departing from Canada. I presume that Canadian citizens will be covered by this provision. The third part of the amendment represents a change in the original act, Section 8.2. This extends the act so it applies to anyone arriving from a place outside Canada. That means all visitors will be subject to the same rules as any resident of Canada who has been abroad.
The main issue I think involves the fact that the act is considerably broader. The number of diseases that are involved is quite limited, but they are important to those who might be afflicted, and important to the health of our people. The act seems to give more latitude to the quarantine officer. Undoubtedly it will cause some unhappiness and a fair amount of conflict when visitors are held under the act. Therefore I think it is important that, when we review the bill at the committee stage, we get answers to some of the difficult questions which may arise. Some of these questions have international overtones, particularly as the measure applies to visitors and immigrants from abroad. Those few words are all I have to say in respect of this bill, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I find it rather difficult to follow three of my colleagues, each of whom is a doctor, and I refer to the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk), the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. Holmes), and the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ritchie). When the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) introduced this bill we were treated to a rather fascinating lesson on the history of the Quarantine Act. It brought to our attention a concern regarding the possibility of contagious and infectious diseases becoming more prevalent in Canada. If this is the fact we should be extremely concerned.
I was very interested to learn of the role the World Health Organization plays in respect of this matter, particularly when it comes to a desire on the part of the federal government to add contagious diseases by way of order in council. I should hope that the minister does consult the World Health Organization before moving in a unilateral way.
The hon. member for Lambton-Kent brought home the necessity of medical research in this area. He pointed out most vividly the necessity for continuing co-operation and the continuing provision of funds in order that we might have the best medical research possible.
What I have found most fascinating about this whole matter is that in his introduction the minister made no mention of the Olympics being held in this country this year. I find this strange, particularly in light of the fact that about a month and a half ago the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) also brought forward a bill because of a concern about the possibility of terrorists coming into the country at the time of the Olympic Games.

This is perhaps also the concern of the Minister of National Health and Welfare, but rather than coming clean he completely ignores this possibility in his introduction of the bill, and says nothing about this means of keeping people out of the country.
Perhaps this bill is part of an Olympic package. The first bill dealt primarily with terrorists and now we have this one which primarily deals with diseases. I hope the minister will enlighten us in this regard, if not here in the House then at the committee. At that time I hope he will be honest with us. I am not suggesting he is less than honest now, but there are some questions that should be answered in order that we may determine why the government is bringing a bill of this type before the House.
Considerable emphasis has been placed on Lassa fever and Marburg disease. Both of these infections have been isolated for some period of time, as pointed out by the hon. member for Lambton-Kent. I wonder why these diseases have been emphasized at this particular time. I suggest the answer is that this is the second part of an Olympic package.
The hon. member for Athabasca in a brilliant speech said that he agreed with the bill in principle, but pointed out there are many questions that have to be answered. The two diseases I mentioned have been known of for some time. That being the case, I wonder why they have not been brought within the Quarantine Act before now. Instead, the minister has waited until almost the time of the Olympic Games and then says he is concerned about the health of Canadians.
What we have here is an extremely powerful bill which actually restricts the movement of people. Some concern has been registered regarding its effect on civil liberties. There is no doubt but that it does have an effect. The explanation to clause 3 states:
The purpose of this amendment is to empower a quarantine officer in emergency situations to take certain action, subject to the approval of the Minister and, where the action involves detention for a period in excess of 48-hours, subject to review by a judge of a superior court, in order to prevent the introduction into Canada of dangerous diseases not presently covered by the Act.
That is the purpose of the main change to this act. It will broaden the section, and I suggest it is a change that we should look into thoroughly when we are considering the bill in committee. As I have suggested, this change affects the freedom of movement and the civil liberties of people. This does not stop with the actions of a quarantine officer. He now has this right when he suspects a disease may be brought into the country. This is peculiar wording and I suggest it defies definition. We will have to look into the definition of the word "suspects". When the quarantine officer has suspicion about a dangerous disease being brought in he has the right to detain individuals.
What is even more important, and this has not been mentioned, but has been alluded to, is the fact that a collector of customs will also be in the same boat. He will also have the awesome power that before now only rested with a quarantine officer. If a customs officer suspects there is a dangerous disease being brought into the country he too can stop the individual and contact the quarantine officer. The quarantine officer must in turn contact the Minister of National Health and Welfare in writing, and
March 29, 1976

the minister must then proceed within 48 hours by way of a superior court judge who will determine the rightness or wrongness of this particular detention. Therefore these matters are of some concern.
I listened to my friend, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), a very respected gentleman in the House, who spoke about the possibility of loss of freedom of movement and also loss of civil liberties. Of course this matter will be looked into more thoroughly by the members on the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs where that concern will be registered, but in keeping with what the government is trying to do because of the Olympic Games which will take place this summer, we all want co-operation. This does not mean to say that we will give the government a blank cheque. It is not the role of the opposition to give governments blank cheques, and particularly this government. I do not want to be partisan on this bill because this bill is for the benefit of all Canadians, and hopefully it will enhance the role played by our country in support of a city which is hosting the Olympic Games.
I believe that we should proceed with caution. We all want to co-operate, but with co-operation comes the necessity to say, "Stop, let us look at what the minister is attempting to do." If we have to ask questions, let us ask what is the opinion of the World Health Organization regarding the procedure proposed by the minister in this bill. What do they think about Lassa fever and Marburg disease? Should it be spelled out by order in council and brought into the bill? I think we must determine whether this is the practice. I believe it is. If the minister can convince our colleagues that it is not, then this matter has been standing for some time because the government does not have the required answers and that is why it was impossible to bring in this bill before now. The minister will have to tell us that.
We must have answers describing how one determines a dangerous disease. How does the customs officer determine this, and how does a quarantine officer determine it? Can the minister give us answers in that regard? We want to know what other criteria will be set to determine a disease, and will this information be passed on to those who have the authority to detain or quarantine people entering the country at ports of entry? This bill is supposed to deal with emergencies, but nowhere in this bill is it spelled out what an emergency is. That is another question which should be answered by the minister once this bill goes to committee.
I heard there is some question as to whether there are enough places with suitable quarantine facilities. I believe the hon. member for Athabasca voiced some concern in that regard. He is of the opinion that there are not enough such places.

Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief. The other place is often criticized with reference to amendments, but once again it has proved that in accordance with the jurisdiction it has, besides taking care of minority rights, it must take a second look at bills which are of a technical nature. In this case it has done so, not only on an important point in reference to the theft of credit cards but also in reference to translation. The Senate was set up to protect minorities and to act as a sort of court of appeal for this Chamber on matters which must be approved expeditiously, such as Bill C-71.
I am glad that the parliamentary secretary said that there is some responsibility and duty on this House to get on with this bill and get it approved because of the attitude today of those who wish to impose distress and evil on society. There is a feeling of what I call the permissive society, and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) has said that he is endeavouring to tighten up the law.
I am not criticizing either the Minister of Justice, the parliamentary secretary or the government, but a situation arose where two people were given bail. One was charged with murder, and the other with attempted murder. Just a short time ago they came from Vancouver to Calgary and murdered a police officer. They then took two females as hostages for 45 hours. It was only due to the good work of
the Calgary police force that those hostages were freed and the matter was settled.
I endorse exactly what the parliamentary secretary says: let us get on with the job.
I should like to say one last word with reference to the Senate. Too often in this place we hear that they have no function, no real jurisdiction, and they are not doing their job. The purpose of the Senate was to set up a group of fairly wise men who could look at the technicalities of legislation received from this House, and I think the Senate is functioning in that regard. We have a large volume of legislation, and we do not have time to examine it carefully. The Senate has done an excellent job in bringing these amendments before the House of Commons, and this proves that we need the Senate and that the constitution has operated for the benefit of Canadians in this regard.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of my speaking at this time on this particular amendment is to try to put on the record some of the unusual things which have happened to this bill.
Feeds Act
The bill was a straightforward housekeeping bill introduced in the Senate, brought into the House, amended in the House and sent back to the Senate, and the Senate sent it back here amended. All I can say is that to any person who is a member of the public-and I might even say a member of this House of Commons-trying to keep track of what is happening to this bill this is an exercise in profundity which can only be described as asinine.
Let me explain what I mean. This bill was a straightforward bill introduced in the Senate. It came to the House, the House amended it and passed the bill. Since both the Senate and the House passed the bill, under the rules of this place and the other place neither House could consider the bill. They could consider just the amendment. I am hopeful that what I am complaining about can go into the record as a suggestion that there should be some way whereby the records of the various members of parliament and of the people across the country trying to follow these debates could be clear enough that we all know what is happening.
All we have before us at the present time is a bill passed out of the Senate on March 6, 1975. That is all we have in the form of a printed bill. However, in addition we have a report from the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) saying that the bill passed out of the Senate on March 6 is contrary to the Bill of Rights. Those of us who follow what happens in this House understand that the minister took this back to the committee and amended the bill so that it would be within the terms of the Bill of Rights. Because this was an amendment of the bill from the Senate, we sent the piece of paper back to the Senate saying that we had amended the bill so that it would be in comformity with the Bill of Rights, and the Senate took it under advisement. The Senate then made their amendments.
The only way to check what the House did on the amendments and what the Senate did on the amendments is to read Votes and Proceedings. I simply say that for those who are much wiser than I who represent just a simple constituency and try to follow what goes on in this House, I think there should be a little better system of co-ordinating the program between the two Houses of parliament so that the public, including members of parliament, would know what is going on in respect of this very involved system in attempting to follow the procedure on this bill which has been before parliament for over a year.
I sympathize with the minister. It must have been a dreadful experience to follow all the ramifications of what went on concerning what this House and the Senate did. I would simply say that the system is cumbersome and crude. We know that our counterparts in the United States have a meeting which allows both their Houses to get together and bring a matter back so that a common bill may be passed by both Houses. I ask in these short remarks, Mr. Speaker, that you recommend to those who know more about the rules and procedures than I do that they try to get a better system so that members of parliament will know what is happening with regard to their legislation. Unless one knows what happens in this House and its committees and in the other place and its committees one does not really know what is going on.

March 29, 1976
Feeds Act
It takes a pretty good student to follow the procedure in respect of this bill. I am not the only one who has found this confusing. Several weeks ago the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers) explained that he did not understand it. When it came to the House the members did not understand it either. I should like to register my complaint neither to the government, the opposition, nor the other place, but in respect of the cumbersomeness of the rules dealing with matters concerning amendments passing from one House to the other.
Basically, when a bill is passed by this House we cannot debate it again. When a bill is passed in the other place they cannot debate it again. We need a simple flexible system whereby the two Houses of parliament can get together and produce some type of amendment for both Houses so that we both have something in front of us and know what we are dealing with. I should like to register these criticisms of what on the surface seem to be a housekeeping bill but actually is a mess when one tries to follow the procedures of this House.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to express my concern about the bill. My concerns were initially expressed before the standing committee which amended the legislation, and which later was amended by the Senate. If hon. members feel they are confused, how do they suppose a new member feels, a new member who is trying to learn the rules and is concerned about the mix-up between the House of Commons and the Senate? We amended parts of the bill. Then the Senate amended parts of the bill and sent them back to the House of Commons for concurrence.
Initially I expressed concern about the position of the small farmer who might have incorporated his farm and who, if found guilty of contravening certain provisions of the Feeds Act, could be fined a stiff fine by the courts. We spend a good deal of time discussing such questions in the Standing Committee on Agriculture.
I want to congratulate the hon. member who is chairman of the Standing Committee on Agriculture for being so patient as we wrestled with this amendment, attempting to break it down in such a way that the small corporate farm would not be treated in the same manner as the larger corporation. It seems that in our amendments we eliminat-

March 29, 1976
Feeds Act
ed the large corporation from any fine other than the maximum of $2,000. This was noted in the Senate and an amendment was made. It was passed back to us in Votes and Proceedings.
Reading from the Senate Debates, Senator Argue said and I quote:
Here we are narrowing it down to corporations found quilty of an indictable offence, and providing for a smaller penalty for a corporation found guilty on summary conviction.
One of the worries of the members of the other place was that by providing for two types of fines, one for an individual and one for a corporation, a farmer who operates a corporation, for example, that mixes feed in the name of himself and perhaps his family-in other words, a very small family corporation-might be caught twice; he might be found guilty as an individual, and then found guilty as a corporation, so that he might perhaps even be placed in bankruptcy.
When one goes across this country he finds various reasons why many small farms have incorporated. Mainly it is for tax reasons or estate purposes. Because of that, there is a great deal of concern. Many of these small family farm operations and corporations today put in their feeds, in their own mix mills, various drugs and proteins, proteins such as urea which requires a thorough mixing. The labelling must be such that it regulates the mixing of urea into feeds in order that only cattle of at least five months or over 400 pounds should use the protein mixture. As well there are such drugs as aeromycin, terramycin, penicillin, arsenline acid and, at one time, DES mixed in foods for a long period of time so that they are thoroughly dispersed.
Under this legislation an inspector of the Department of Agriculture can go on a farm at will, take a sample of the feed, and have it analysed. Upon analysis it is possible he will find the feed has been improperly mixed. If he feels it would endanger the animals on the individual farm or a neighbour's farm, he could place the individual or corporation under indictment. This is of great concern to me.
I hope the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) will clarify this position and that, even with the Senate amendment, the small corporate farmer will not be treated in the same manner as the large corporation. As I read the amendment I am not sure that is so. I have read it over a number of times. We dealt with it in the agricultural committee. I still feel there is some concern.
The other concern is for small corporations which may only have a staff of one or two individuals. The manager of the corporation may also be involved in the mixing of feed. If his feed is tested by an inspector, analysed, and something is found to be deficient, the inspector can say to the manager of the corporation that there is a problem, and for some reason or other it involves a number of firms and a charge is brought forward.
Under this act, we are zeroing in on managers of corporations. This is all well and good for large corporations such as Swift and Purina, but it is of serious concern to the hundreds of small feed mill operators in western Canada, Ontario, Quebec, and the maritimes. I want to raise this query before we allow the bill to pass. I hope the Minister of Agriculture will relate this to his officials and, in the regulations, they will adhere to the difference between the small corporate feed mill or farm as compared to the large corporation which the Senate is attempting to get at when it amended our amendment wherein we limited the fine to
$2,000. That is the intervention I wish to make tonight before the bill passes on and is given Royal Assent.

subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT (NO. 1), 1976 MEASURES FOR BETTER PROTECTION OF CANADIAN SOCIETY AGAINST CRIME

speechtext: The House resumed, from Thursday, March 11, consideration of the motion of Mr. Basford that Bill C-83, for the better protection of Canadian society against perpetrators of violence and other crime, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.

subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT (NO. 1), 1976 MEASURES FOR BETTER PROTECTION OF CANADIAN SOCIETY AGAINST CRIME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak in favour of the amendment presented on March 9 by my hon. friend from Calgary North respecting Bill C-83. His motion is certainly deserving of the consideration and approval of the House. It asks that the bill not be read a second time, but that its subject matter be referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs for study.
The hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) pointed out most eloquently that the 76 page bill should be split, as 39 pages of the bill deal with new gun laws. This is another case of the government bringing in an omnibus or umbrella bill with a mixture of good legislation and bad, and hoping to sneak the entire package through by serving it all up on one platter.
This bill with its gun controls, broader wire-tapping powers for police, and tougher prison provisions, overlooks the real crime problem. When I compare the opening remarks of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) on March 8 with the substance of Bill C-83 I find it difficult to believe that he and I are talking about the same thing. The minister opened his remarks with the statement that this bill represents major legislative initiative on the part of the government. I suggest that the minister's attempts to rewrite the dictionary have had the same unhappy result as the government's attempts to deal effectively with rising crime in our country.
Bill C-83 is a mish-mash, a hodge-podge, and a patchwork quilt of every conceivable sort of dodge that the minister could come up with in order to avoid facing this issue head on. The excellent rebuttal of this bill by my able colleague shows all too clearly that the Minister of Justice

March 29, 1976
Measures Against Crime
has given us a mixed bag of tricks calculated to throw us off the scent. He and some of his fellow ministers are so determined that no murderer shall hang, or even suffer any real hardship, that they are prepared to sacrifice principle, and even to chip away at the rights of the law-abiding citizen to accomplish that purpose.
The minister went on to say that this bill is designed to ensure the adequate protection of the safety and security of the law-abiding, and the legal rights and dignity of those charged with offences. This is the best indication we could have that the minister has not changed his stripes. He is just as determined as ever to place his own personal convictions above those of the majority of members of parliament and above the wishes of the majority of Canadians. By all means, he says, let us ensure that the rights and dignity of offenders are protected. This is not the same as saying that the rights of all Canadians to full protection of the law should be preserved and protected. The minister should have said that this legislation is designed to protect the safety, security, and legal rights and dignity of the law-abiding.
My sympathies are, and have always been with those who are law-abiding and with those who are the victims of crime. I consider the dignity of the law-abiding to be infinitely more important than the dignity of those who are convicted of crimes, especially those who are convicted of violent crimes. If we can ensure that the dignity of all Canadians will be served by a particular piece of legislation, then let us by all means consider that possibility. But, Mr. Speaker, let us not place the cart before the horse. Let us first do what we must to protect the dignity of those Canadians who respect our system and our laws and who abide by our laws.
The Minister of Justice tells us that the safety and security of law-abiding Canadians will be enhanced by making it more difficult for law-abiding people to obtain and keep rifles and shotguns. In the same breath the minister urges us to approve legislation making it more difficult for people to obtain and keep automatic weapons, pistols, and such weapons as sawed-off rifles and shotguns. For the life of me I cannot make the connection between those weapons designed purely for criminal use, and those designed for, and used by, hunters and sportsmen. I am not talking about the types of pistols used by sportsmen for target shooting or by our Olympic shooting teams. These guns are required to be registered, and it is my understanding that permits are only issued for these pistols to persons known to be of good character and who do not have records of criminal activity.
What I am talking about is the registration of every person in Canada who wants to own a shotgun or rifle. In the first place it is a matter of record that no country in the western world has been able to prevent people from owning guns simply by outlawing them. It is also well known that one of the first things that a communist government does when it takes over a country is to outlaw the ownership of guns, any kind of gun, and the penalty for owning a gun in most of those countries is death.
History has shown that oppressive laws only breed lawbreakers. In some countries like Sweden, Israel, and
France, oppressive tax laws have served only to develop a nation of tax cheats. A story in a local paper recently pointed out that the government of France collects only about one half of taxes actually owed, and it noted that the Frenchman and Frenchwoman who is not a tax cheat is a rarity. The same syndrome can be detected in countries where there are oppressive laws concerning the ownership of guns. A veteran police official in Britain, where gun laws are extremely strict, said that there are millions of unregistered guns in Britain, and he also said that there simply was not any way that anyone could ferret out these illegal guns.
The city of Detroit probably has the strictest gun laws on this continent, yet I need not point out that Detroit is the murder capital of North America and that the majority of murders in that city are committed with guns, restricted guns-outlawed guns, if you will. By comparison, in the deep south of the U.S. where anybody can own a gun of any type, except for automatic weapons, the per capita murder rate with guns is significantly lower than in cities where restrictive gun laws are in force.
May I just put some statistics on the record, Mr. Speaker. In 1973, 474 murders were committed; in 1974, there were 545 murders. Less than half this number in each year were committed with guns. I point out that in 1973, 56 murders were committed with a handgun; in 1974, the number was 71. There were 114 murders committed with a rifle in 1973 and 122 in 1974. Sawed-off rifles accounted for two murders in 1973 and six in 1974. Sawed-off shotguns accounted for three murders in 1974 only, none in 1973. Shotguns were used in 31 murders in 1973, and in 55 murders in 1974. In 1973, 11 murders were committed using a gun of an unknown type; in 1974 the number was 15. In other words, in the majority of murders some weapon other than a gun was used-for example, beatings, stabbings, strangulation, suffocation, drowning, axing; and in some cases cause of death was unknown.
What I am trying to say is that we in Canada cannot outlaw the instruments of death any more than we can outlaw death itself. If we could outlaw violent death, then I would suggest that the government use its majority in this House to do just that. That would be more reasonable and just than to use its majority to push this bill through the House. The Minister of Justice takes liberties with our intelligence when he suggests that we are in the process of outlawing the instruments of death by agreeing to impose licensing requirements and restrictions on all law-abiding Canadian gun owners.
A friend of mine, when I was speaking to him at a banquet last Saturday night and happened to mention the possibility that this very important and contentious gun control legislation would be before the House this week, stated that he could make a weapon, which I presume could be classed as a gun. He described how he could make it out of a piece of pipe and this, that, and the other thing, at a cost of 75 cents, and that he could make it in less than an hour. This is further proof that anyone who has the desire to murder will be able to do so using some type of weapon.
Let us take the various aspects of this part of the legislation and apply hypothetical situations to them and see just how ridiculous they appear in the clear light of day. I refer

March 29, 1976

hon. members to the first step, the establishment of a nation-wide bureaucracy of gun licensing agencies employing thousands of persons. These people will be given a frightening degree of latitude by this legislation to approve or reject applications from citizens who want to keep the guns they now own or to obtain new guns. I am talking about rifles and shotguns only.
Then pile on top of that the mountains of paper work that must be processed and forwarded to central record offices. In addition we must have an elaborate appeal procedure to protect the rights of citizens from arbitrary decisions made by bureaucrats. This begins to get more and more expensive, Mr. Speaker, and will enable the government to reward more and more of the party faithful, defeated candidates, and friends ad infinitum. Perhaps this is the way that the Minister of Justice plans to justify the enormous expense.
May I call it ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker.
A motion to adjourn the House under Standing Order 40 deemed to have been moved.

subtopic: FISHERIES-SEALS-REQUEST FOR TABLING OF REPORT ON DECLINE IN POPULATION AND NEED FOR DECREASING QUOTAS
FISHERIES-SEALS-REQUEST FOR TABLING OF REPORT ON DECLINE IN POPULATION AND NEED FOR DECREASING QUOTAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 1 I asked the Minister of State (Fisheries) (Mr. LeBlanc) two questions concerning seals and sealing on the east coast of Canada. The questions related to the tabling of an interim report to the minister from the committee on seals and sealing, and the studies by his department on alternative employment for persons who would be affected by a phasing out or stoppage or serious curtailment of the seal hunt. The minister's answers to these questions, is the reason I am debating the issue this evening. I wish I had 70 minutes, Mr. Speaker, instead of the seven minutes limitation that is imposed upon me.
In the July, 1974, election campaign many Canadians obtained a written or oral commitment from most political candidates that if they were elected they would ask the government to find ways and means of stopping the senseless slaughter of the seals and, at the same time, find alternative means of income for those who were affected by such stoppage. The concerned Canadians who opposed the seal hunt had three main reasons-first, the serious depletion of the seal herd; second, the method of killing the seals; and third, the minimum income obtained by the sealers.
The interim report of the committee on seals and sealing, which was composed of representatives from the animal welfare, scientific, and industrial communities, and was
Adjournment Debate
not aligned with any government agency, studied the seal hunt in Canada with regard to conservation aspects and humane killing methods. May I quote from the report regarding some of its findings. Having regard to the conservation aspects the report states at page 2;
The one definite conclusion based on scientific analyses of available data between 1950 and 1970 is that the stock of harp seals has been halved. The original size of the seal population although of interest statistically, is immaterial in considering this point. The population trend towards decrease is continuing. This decrease in population has been supported by observations made by vessel-borne sealers, landsmen, government officials, casual observers, and biologists. There has been some difference of opinion on the effect of reducing the size of the annual kill on the recovery rate of the seal herd. Only continuing research can ensure the herd is not eradicated.
If the seal hunt is maintained at the 1972 level there will be a total elimination of the one year old animals in 2014. The harp seal would then move toward extinction as the older animals die off. A decrease in the annual exploitation of the harp seal is therefore indicated if the species is to survive.
A moratorium in 1973 on the taking of seals, except for those taken by the aboriginal population (native human populations of the Canadian Arctic and Greenland), would allow the herd to start its recovery in
1975.	If the seal hunt is phased out, by all but aboriginals, over the period 1972-1974 then the herd will start to substantially recover in
1976.	The phase out is preferable as it has obvious advantages to the sealer, as well as to the government in allowing the latter to implement economic support for these changes.
On page 6 of the report this committee summarizes by a number points as follows;
1. The majority of the Committee on Seals and Sealing supports a phasing out of the Canadian and Norwegian harp and hood seal hunt...
3.	The phase out must be accompanied by an economic evaluation of the change in income to the sealer, vessel owner and operator and the processing plant operator, so as to prevent individual hardship.
4.	Intensified research, through contract and governmental laboratories, must be carried out to ensure satisfactory guidelines for protection of the harp and hood seal population, if these species are ever again exploited.
5.	The sealer, when advised, has made every attempt to act humanely in the killing of seals. There is no reason to believe he is in any way different in his attitude to the killing of animals from any other human being.
What has been the response of the minister? There has been no real phase out with regard to the seal hunt. There has been a slight reduction from 150,000 to 125,000 for the 1976 seal hunt. There has been no evaluation of the incomes loss to the sealers or the finding of alternative employment. There has been no research as to other methods of killing seals. There has been no research as to the effect of the eating habits of the seals on other marine life, and there has been no indication of the termination of the sealing agreement between Canada and Norway, and the necessity of giving three years notice with regard to its termination. In other words there has been no real response by the minister to these very vital issues.
What has been the response of most Canadians? There has been disappointment at the continuation of the senseless slaughter of seals for the maximum profit of the Norwegian industry which caters to the vanity of European women in a luxury trade. There has been concern that the government should pit sealers against other Canadians regarding loss of income to sealers, instead of finding alternative methods of earning income for the sealers. There has also been the necessity of the Greenpeace Foundation to dramatize the problem to the govern-

March 29, 1976
Adjournment Debate
ment, instead of the government and members of parliament finding ways and means to solve the problem.
I am asking the minister to stop dividing Canadians on the social, moral and financial issues and to direct his mind and manpower to finding a solution to the conservation of the seals, alternative humane methods of killing, and the protection of income and the safety of the sealers. If he does this he will gain the respect and admiration of all Canadians.

speakeroldname: Mr. George Baker (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subtopic: FISHERIES-SEALS-REQUEST FOR TABLING OF REPORT ON DECLINE IN POPULATION AND NEED FOR DECREASING QUOTAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is no single report directed to the subject of current population levels of the seal herds. There are many recent scientific reports by Canadian and Norwegian scientists on the harp seal populations. These differ in content and conclusions.
It should be noted that at least four species of seals on the Atlantic coast are being hunted. The status of the various seal populations and the regulations under which they are harvested differ for each species.
The harbour seal and the grey seal are resident in Canadian waters the year round, and their activities in destroying fish and fishermen's gear are a serious problem in some areas. For this reason the department operates a bounty program to encourage the cropping of harbour seals, and itself undertakes and annual cull of grey seals, that is, the latter herds are thinned out by departmental officers to keep their numbers in check.
The species which are hunted commercially are the harp seal and the hooded seal. The abundance levels and population biology of the hooded seal are not well known, and the harvest has been held at a maximum 15,000 for the past five years. In 1976 Canadian hunters were allotted 6,000 and Norwegian hunters 9,000.
The species which is in greatest abundance is the harp seal and the main commercial harvest is directed toward this animal. It is a significant predator of fish and thereby a significant competitor of fishermen. At current population levels it is estimated to consume about one million tons of fish and smaller marine animals annually, including a quarter of a million tons of capelin-itself a significant food item of other fish species, and also of our people. '
Like the hooded seal, the harp is not present year round in Canadian waters, but is present during its breeding season in late winter and spring. During this period it consumes 10 to 15 thousand tons of herring in the gulf of St. Lawrence alone.
The harp seal has been hunted commercially for hundreds of years, not only in the Northwestern Atlantic, but in the White sea and other places near Spitzbergen in the Northeastern Atlantic. All these herds have fluctuated in size over the years, and have, at one time or another, experienced over-exploitation. In the Northwestern Atlantic the harp seal is hunted in spring by ship-based hunters from Norway and Canada, and by land-based hunters in Newfoundland and the Magdalen Islands. At other times of the year it is taken at Labrador, the Canadian Arctic, and West Greenland by resident fishermen and hunters.
The harp seal appears to have been over-exploited at several times during the long history of the seal hunt in the Northwestern Atlantic, most recently in the 1960's. The

hunt came under international regulation, International Commission for the Northwest Atlantic Fisheries- ICNAF, in 1967. An initial quota of 245,000 in 1971 was reduced to 150,000 in 1972 to 1975, and to 127,000 in 1976.
Excessive exploitation in the 1960's and earlier has resulted in declines in pup production in the 1970's. Lower levels of pup production may be expected until the beneficial effects of the quotas from 1972 onwards become evident in 1978 onwards, since the seals mature at about age six. Meanwhile the hunt is being regulated to prevent further decline in the herds. The herd is now estimated at about one million animals.
