subtopic: AGRICULTURE-EFFECT ON EXPORT TRADE OF REMOVAL OF TRANSPORTATION SUBSIDY ON FLOUR-GOVERNMENT ACTION
AGRICULTURE-EFFECT ON EXPORT TRADE OF REMOVAL OF TRANSPORTATION SUBSIDY ON FLOUR-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question directed to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) on March 19 concerned the impact of the removal of the transportation subsidy on grain and flour shipped from east coast ports which constitutes a serious threat to an important industry and is a policy decision which, I believe, should be reconsidered by the government.
The minister in his answer left the impression that the flour milling industry for export purposes is a dying enterprise. He implied that it is better for us as a nation to ship the raw product, in this case wheat, rather than worrying about processing it in the form of flour. I must advise him for his information that some markets for grain can only be met by the export of flour. For example, Africa, and the nations in the West Indies do not have any flour milling capacity, and so therefore the exports we ship in the form of wheat have to be made in this case in the form of flour.
It is interesting to note that Canada mills approximately 90 million bushels a year. In the face of this the sort of shallow attitude of the Liberal government has led Canada into a major slump in manufacturing trade which is now causing us to slide into a major crisis. This attitude has resulted in our country facing a very serious trade deficit. In 1975 there was a deficit of some $8 billion in the so-called higher technology manufacturing field. That was $1 billion worse than it was the year before, and more than three times the sum of what it was in 1970. This means lost jobs, lost economic activity, lost investment activity, lost potential for technological achievement and, in short, lost opportunities for present and future generations of Canadians.
I am told that the elimination of this subsidy could mean a loss to Canada of something in the order of $28 million worth of value added processing activities, or a total economic spin-off of something in the order of $65 million.
Let us look at the flour trade and what has happened in Canada relative to the world position, and let us examine for a moment what effect this government decision will have upon its future.
March 29, 1976

First, world demand for flour has expanded from 65 million hundredweight in 1954 to 95 million hundredweight in 1974, an increase of 50 per cent. Canada's share, meanwhile, declined from 31 per cent to 11 per cent. In 1954 Canadian millers were exporting 20 million hundredweight. In 1964 we exported 24 million hundredweight on an annual basis, and in 1975 our exports dropped by more than 50 per cent from the 1954 figure, to a figure of 8.5 million hundredweight, and by 65 per cent since the 1964 figure.
The minister suggests that more and more countries are milling their own flour. Well, for his information, only Canada and Australia have experienced substantial declines in exports of flour. The U.S. share has not fallen appreciably from its level of 1954. As a matter of fact, until 1972 it was well above its 1954 level. The European Common Market, meanwhile, has expanded its exports over a period of ten years from 15 million hundredweight to 64 million hundredweight in 1974. Therefore it is categorically wrong to suggest that world export demand for flour has fallen. As I pointed out earlier, some countries have no flour milling capacity so the only way our grain can enter those countries is in the form of flour.
The actions which are proposed by the government in abolishing this freight subsidy will only serve to worsen an already deteriorating Canadian industry and will result in further declines in our share of the export flour trade. In this instance I do not believe that the government has carried out an accurate cost benefit analysis, and I suggested that it do just that before proceeding further. The result of this action by the government will increase freight costs to Canadian millers by 212 per cent. This cost will have to be added to the export price of flour.
We are told by the Canadian National Millers' Association that while the U.S.S.R. has indicated requirements for
375,000	tons of Canadian flour during 1976, it has insisted that further negotiations be conducted in the event of freight costs are to be adjusted upward. The U.S.S.R. representatives have stated further that Canada is no longer competitive in world markets and that further price increases will require them to look for alternative suppliers.
The Canadian National Millers' Association sums up its observations as follows:
Eliminating the subsidy and the "hold-down* will visit disaster upon Canadian millers and damage a substantial export market for Canadian wheat in the form of flour. We cannot believe that these and other foreseeable consequences are in the public interest.
I urge the minister to persuade his cabinet colleagues to reconsider this policy. I suggest that an immediate cost benefit analysis be undertaken, and if it is revealed that such a subsidy should be discontinued, something which I doubt, then I suggest that it be discontinued in a phase out period over the next four or five years so that the industry can adjust over a period of time rather than be disrupted by a spontaneous government action.
I do not believe the action which is contemplated by the government in the form of restraint program is in the public interest at this time. I believe it will only serve to accentuate the speedy demise of Canada's already shaken and eroded flour industry. I must say in conclusion that the whole restraint program which has been advocated by the government plays too harshly with agriculture. I think
Adjournment Debate
agriculture under this restraint program is getting short shrift.

speakeroldname: Mr. Irenee Pelletier (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: AGRICULTURE-EFFECT ON EXPORT TRADE OF REMOVAL OF TRANSPORTATION SUBSIDY ON FLOUR-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, part of the initial rationale for the "At and East" subsidy was to keep an all-Canadian route competitive with the American alternative. American rates have increased significantly since that time and current indications are that a full compensatory level in Canada would be preferable to other alternatives. However, as the subsidy has been in effect for some time its removal will result in some adjustment for Canadian flour exporters.
As the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) mentioned, there has been a general movement in most countries toward milling their own wheat. To the extent that Canada has replaced some of our flour exports with wheat exports these markets have not been lost. The world export market for flour has been stagnant since the late fifties with an increasing share of the market going to lower quality, subsidized EEC flour. In spite of substantial PL480 activity even American sales have dropped dramatically.
Canadian flour exports fall into three categories: first, commercial; second, government; and, third, Russia-Cuba. The bulk of these sales are made to Cuba under the Russian sales agreements for Canadian grain. The removal of the subsidy will not affect sales in 1976. In the longer run it is expected that Cuba will move toward a higher degree of self-sufficiency in wheat milling. Until that time the government will continue its efforts to maintain this market.
Commercial sales and sales to the Canadian government together accounted for the balance of flour exports-about 25 per cent. Sales to the government will likely continue at present levels regardless of the subsidy. Commercial sales may be effected. However, a strong case has not been made by the Canadian National Millers' Association as to the magnitude of these effects. The Department of Agriculture is keeping a close watch on this situation and if other aspects arise appropriate action will be taken.

subtopic: REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-INQUIRY WHETHER THERE ARE ANY PLANS FOR PORT OF PICTOU, NOVA SCOTIA
REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-INQUIRY WHETHER THERE ARE ANY PLANS FOR PORT OF PICTOU, NOVA SCOTIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to pursue further the question I raised earlier this month with the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard) concerning whether or not DREE has any concrete plans or projects, either by itself or in concert with other federal agencies in the province of Nova Scotia, for development assistance for the port of Pictou.
I know that we are in a time of restraint in government spending, but that, I submit, does not or should not apply to essential infrastructure projects. I realize that priprities must be constantly re-examined. However, I submit that there is a good case to be made for more DREE involvement in developing the port of Pictou. At least we must begin some systematic efforts to improve matters.
This once busy and still strategic port is immediately adjacent to a heavily industrialized infrastructure including Hawker Siddeley, pulp and paper mills, Scott Pulp,

Adjournment Debate
Michelin Tire, Ferguson Industries, shipbuilding and so on, together with several small industries. These are important industrial components of the complex which ships all over the world and needs proved access to salt water in order to realize its full potential.
This is not the first time I have pointed out to the minister and to his predecessor, now the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Jamieson), that Pictou county in general and the port of Pictou have been neglected, and that DREE by itself and in conjunction with other federal departments such as Public Works and Transport ought to and indeed must make a meaningful effort to upgrade this port for the good of the area and its people.
This month the minister, in response to my request for support in my representations to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cullen) to keep open the customs office in Pictou, stated that he was advised the volume of business would not justify my request to the Minister of National Revenue being granted. This is indeed a retrogade step because now the port of Pictou can no longer act as a ships' registry. Surely this ought to give the minister and the government an additional reason for improving the port. Once it is improved, the business will come to it.
Earlier this winter I got in touch with civic officials, business executives, and other prominent and interested persons in Pictou county, to ask for their opinions and support in making the government in general and the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion in particular aware of the need for better marine facilities at Pictou. I received that support from the mayors of several towns, and received an offer of assistance from the Pictou County Research and Development Commission.
In the limited time available I wish to put on record some excerpts from communications sent to me by some of the mayors of towns which, together, make up this important industrial area.
Mr. R. J. Murae, Mayor of Stellarton, wrote in part:
I wish to assure you of my complete co-operation on your endeavour to improve port facilities in Pictou. It is something that is long past due. I propose to have a resolution passed by our council and forwarded to you immediately.
Walter Duggan, Mayor of Westville, wrote:
It is our feeling that any development to the port facilities would not only benefit the town of Pictou, but the county as a whole.
M. A. Harquail, Mayor of New Glasgow, wrote:
Pictou county has a great need for industrial and economic expansion. Industrial expansion without ready access to markets, is, as you are aware, a case of putting the cart before the horse. For this reason I endorse your efforts and offer my support.
The mayor of Pictou, Mr. Clarence McCarthy, sent out many detailed examples of how Pictou would benefit from and is entitled to more funding to increase its capability as a port. I forwarded his excellent letter to the minister as I did with the other letters. I wish to put part of his representation on public record in Hansard so that people of Pictou will see where he stands on their behalf. The mayor said in part:
Mention is made of the ice locked condition of the harbour during the winter months as being a deterrent. To counteract this one should look back to the war years when the port was a most important repair depot for the Royal Canadian Navy every month of the year, and Foundation Maritime Limited were building . . . 2,400-ton steel freighters and sending them to sea, once each month, 24 in all.
If we consider the freeze-up as a reason for non-use of the harbour oy our Pictou county manufacturers it could be an argument that storage sheds with enough capacity to carry over this freeze-up period are needed; incorporated as well could be capacity for at least... 12,000 tons of feed grain which would be transported from the Lakehead before freeze-up. Surely this would allow for cheaper feed than the present method of storing a rail shipment of only ... 200 tons at Scotsburn.
It is obvious that we are not using the port of Pictou to its best advantage.
Pictou county has recently received assistance in the form of DREE grants made to businesses in the area. We recognize this and appreciate it. As member for the area, may I, too, express my appreciation. But unlike the "grand centres" encompassing the Halifax-Dartmouth area, or the strait area of Nova Scotia, we have received little if any of the type of infrastructure aid to which we are entitled. For example, $20 million was committed in 1972 for the Metropolitan Area Growth Investment Organization in the Halifax-Dartmouth metropolitan area. To date this investment has produced little if any benefit because of the delays arising in handling. The interest paid on this money in three years would be more than enough to pay for the facilities which the port of Pictou desperately requires.
In conclusion I ask the minister to make a commitment to provide more infrastructure aid in Pictou county and to improve the port of Pictou. This will bring quick rewards in promoting a better way of life and expansion of business. The people of Pictou county have always shown an ability to respond to opportunity. They deserve a more equitable share of federal moneys spent in Nova Scotia for infrastructure assistance.
I hope the minister will give my representation favourable consideration. I repeat that this important area of Nova Scotia has not received its fair share of infrastructure aid. It has not received that kind of assistance to which I referred in my question earlier this month.

speakeroldname: Mr. Cliff Mclsaac (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion
subtopic: REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-INQUIRY WHETHER THERE ARE ANY PLANS FOR PORT OF PICTOU, NOVA SCOTIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as usual the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) ably delineated his concern for his region. He was able to quote from letters sent by people in Pictou and neighbouring communities which support his position.
I am aware that Pictou has a great tradition as a shipbuilding centre and as an active port over the years. To my knowledge, the Department of Regional Economic Expansion was not directly approached by the government of Nova Scotia about further planning or funding for port development at Pictou.
As I am sure the hon. member is aware, the development of port facilities falls under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Transport. I am not offering that to dodge any responsibility from the point of view of DREE. DREE has provided industrial incentives to a number of firms in Pictou. It is my understanding also that our officials anticipate a further proposal from a firm in that area in the fairly immediate future.
It is certainly the intention of DREE to make full use of all of the development instruments available to provide co-operation and full support for initiatives undertaken by the province, by other federal departments, or by the private sector to help the port of Pictou achieve its full potential and at least some of its former greatness, of which the hon. member is well aware.
